articles.title: Drone delivers food to chimpanzee cut off by flooding
articles.summary: Drone video shows the animal retrieving food from a paper bag dropped nearby after flooding blocked access to a Florida chimpanzee sanctuary.
articles.body:
A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary that provides lifelong care for animals formerly used in research laboratories, the pet trade and the entertainment industry was hit by flooding that left roads impassable. Staff used a drone to deliver food to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee cut off from access. The non-profit facility said despite floodwaters damaging roads, buildings and equipment, staff closely monitored and cared for the animals.

articles.title: Fux suspende processos sobre proibição das bets até STF decidir sobre validade da medida | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão vale para ações que tramitam nas instâncias inferiores da Justiça e discutem constitucionalidade da MP do governo Lula. Ministro atendeu a pedido do procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet.
articles.summary: Decisão vale para ações que tramitam nas instâncias inferiores da Justiça e discutem constitucionalidade da MP do governo Lula. Ministro atendeu a pedido do procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet.
articles.body:
O ministro Luiz Fux , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), determinou a suspensão, em todo o país, de todos os processos que tramitam nas instâncias inferiores da Justiça e discutem a constitucionalidade da medida provisória (MP) que proibiu as bets no Brasil.

A decisão, datada deste domingo (8), vale até que o STF julgue definitivamente as ações que questionam a medida . Fux é relator de quatro ações diretas de inconstitucionalidade sobre a MP na Corte.

➡️ O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) publicou, em 25 de setembro, a MP que proibiu a exploração, a oferta, a intermediação e a publicidade das apostas de quota fixa no país, além de jogos on-line e cassinos virtuais.

Fux atendeu a um pedido apresentado na sexta-feira (6) pelo procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet . O chefe da PGR argumentou que decisões divergentes de instâncias inferiores estavam gerando insegurança jurídica e fazendo com que a proibição fosse aplicada de forma desigual pelo país ( entenda mais abaixo ).

Na decisão, Fux afirmou que há risco de múltiplas decisões em sentidos diferentes enquanto o próprio Supremo analisa a validade da MP.

Para o ministro, estão presentes os requisitos necessários para paralisar as ações até uma definição da Corte.

Fux afirmou que o debate sobre as bets envolve uma questão constitucional que já foi colocada para análise do STF.

“Há o risco de insegurança jurídica em decorrência da possibilidade de múltiplas decisões em sentidos divergentes, com o agravante de se tratar de potencial liberação de atividade reconhecidamente danosa e de elevado risco social, qual seja a exploração de apostas de quota fixa — como tive a oportunidade de me manifestar na audiência pública realizada no dia 03.11.2026, bem como em meu voto no RE 966.177/RS, na Sessão do Plenário do dia 06.08.2026”, escreveu o ministro.

Na prática, juízes e tribunais de instâncias inferiores terão de paralisar os processos que questionam a validade da MP que proibiu as bets no Brasil.

Esses casos ficarão suspensos até que o STF decida se a proibição é constitucional.

A decisão foi tomada apenas por Luiz Fux e ainda terá de ser analisada pelos demais ministros do Supremo, que poderão mantê-la ou derrubá-la.

Ao justificar a suspensão nacional, Fux afirmou que a MP já é alvo de quatro ações diretas de inconstitucionalidade no STF e que decisões tomadas em outros tribunais poderiam produzir entendimentos diferentes enquanto o Supremo não dá a palavra final.

O ministro mencionou ainda o risco de decisões que permitam a retomada das apostas. Segundo Fux, trata-se de uma atividade de "elevado risco social".

O ministro já havia manifestado posição contrária às bets durante audiência pública realizada pelo STF em 3 de novembro. Na ocasião , Fux disse que sua "percepção" era de que as apostas deveriam ser banidas .

O ministro fez ressalva, no entanto, de que essa avaliação não encerrava a análise jurídica da MP do governo, que envolve questões como segurança jurídica, proteção da confiança das empresas autorizadas a operar e a existência dos requisitos de relevância e urgência necessários para uma medida provisória.

Ministro Luiz Fux — Foto: Victor Piemonte/STF

O pedido de Paulo Gonet ocorreu após decisões de instâncias inferiores que permitiram que empresas específicas voltassem a oferecer apostas apesar da MP.

No documento, Fux citou uma liminar da Justiça Federal de São Paulo que permitiu que a Stake Brazil continuasse operando temporariamente e uma decisão que suspendeu os efeitos da MP para o grupo CDA Gaming, responsável pelas plataformas Casa de Apostas, Betsul e Jogo Online.

Na sexta, porém, o presidente do Tribunal Regional Federal da 3ª Região (TRF-3) derrubou a autorização que havia permitido às três plataformas da CDA Gaming voltar a funcionar.

Ao tomar a decisão, afirmou que a controvérsia sobre as bets já estava sob análise do STF e que seria inconveniente que instâncias inferiores antecipassem entendimentos sobre o tema.

A discussão começou depois que o governo do presidente Lula publicou, no fim de setembro, a MP que proibiu a exploração, a oferta, a intermediação e a publicidade das apostas de quota fixa no país.

A proibição também atingiu jogos on-line e cassinos virtuais. Os sites começaram a ser bloqueados em 6 de outubro.

Entidades do setor recorreram ao STF. A Associação Nacional de Jogos e Loterias (ANJL) e o Instituto Brasileiro de Jogo Responsável (IBJR) argumentam, entre outros pontos, que a interrupção das atividades gera insegurança jurídica para empresas que haviam recebido autorização do próprio governo para operar.

As operadoras afirmam que pagaram R$ 30 milhões por licença e fizeram investimentos para atender às regras do mercado regulado.

A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), por outro lado, defende a manutenção da proibição e afirma que há razões econômicas, sociais e de saúde para a medida.

Na semana passada, Fux realizou uma audiência pública para reunir argumentos sobre o tema. O debate subsidiará a análise de oito ações no Supremo: quatro contra a MP que proibiu as apostas on-line e outras quatro relacionadas à legislação que regulamentou o setor.

Na ocasião, não havia data definida para julgamento.

articles.title: Congress returns to brutal lame-duck stretch with shutdown deadline, leadership races: 'Closet is full of s—'
articles.summary: Lawmakers return to Capitol Hill facing a government shutdown deadline, the farm bill and a debt ceiling fight before Democrats take power in January.
articles.body: Lawmakers are back on Capitol Hill this week for the first time since the midterm elections, and Republicans have a slew of responsibilities in front of them before Democrats take over the reins of power in January. "The lame duck is like that closet in your house where everybody's throwing a bunch of s--- into it," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. "And the closet is full of s--- now, and now we got to figure out how to get it all out of there." Current federal funding levels run out on Dec. 11, and without another deal in place, Congress risks plunging the government into another shutdown. Some Democrats signaled to POLITICO that they could use President Donald Trump’s war in Iran as leverage in spending talks — which could very well lead to a fiscal cliff that could paralyze federal agencies. But one House Republican, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told Fox News Digital they expect another short-term extension of current funding levels, called a continuing resolution (CR), through February or March of next year. The current CR was passed to cover the end of the last fiscal year ending Sept. 30 through next month. TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "No one wants a shutdown, I would think," that House Republican said. "Not even Dems." HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS Other legislative priorities Congress will have to reckon with in the next few weeks include the farm bill, which is passed every five years and sets food and agriculture policy for the country. Republicans are also aiming to pass a bill to revitalize the country’s transportation infrastructure and a bipartisan tax package before the end of the year. Then there is also the looming debt ceiling deadline coming in January, which Trump will likely call on Republicans to deal with before Congress changes hands. GOP lawmakers shared varying levels of optimism when asked about how productive they would be. "It can be. It should be," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., said. "But my faith in some of my Senate colleagues is not real high, because I feel like they have a personal vendetta towards the president, and it's more about that than it is about passing legislation. We should do our business in Congress." Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, said, "I think it's gonna be difficult to get a whole lot done. But we have done a lot of work leading up to the lame-duck session to prepare for passing a number of important bills, many of which are bipartisan." But first, both House and Senate Republicans will need to face their losses in person — and consider how to rebuild. WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL "It’s going to feel like a funeral," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "It’s depressing even for those of us who won, because we lost so many good, quality members." The first order of business this week will be choosing their new leaders for the next Congress. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running for the minority leader role unopposed for now. And House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is vying for the minority leader role against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS But Moran and Stutzman both said Republicans would unify quickly after that drama is resolved. "It should be immediate," Stutzman said. "If we're not paying attention to the American people, and we're focusing on leadership positions and personality fights, we're gonna continue to lose." HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES DEFENSE PLAN TO SHIELD TRUMP FROM LOOMING DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATIONS Moran said, "We understand now more than ever how important it is for us to come back together, coalesce and to regroup for the next election, and to prepare for the defense of democracy." On Democrats’ side, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to glide into the speaker role after leading his party to a commanding victory. Democrats’ leadership elections will take place the week after Republicans’ do. And on the productivity front, Stutzman also called on the Senate to pass the election security-focused SAVE America Act, which Republicans are attempting to accomplish via the budget reconciliation process to sidestep the need for Democrat support. The House passed a blueprint for the bill in July. Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has been working on the structure of that package for some time, but wasn’t so sure that if Republicans lost, it would be something the GOP had the political will to finish. "It might turn to some people's attitudes in terms of support for it," Johnson said. Then there’s permitting reform, which was on thin ice heading into Election Night until the White House and Senate Democrats struck a deal for a variety of wind projects to move forward. Whether Democrats support that now, and give Trump and the GOP a win on their way out, remains to be seen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China spy scandal?
articles.summary: Allegations linking CEO to Chinese intelligence shake markets with chipmaker’s shares falling more than 4 percent.
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions over allegations that a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had a romantic relationship was gathering intelligence for Beijing.

Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe United States national security or confidential information has been compromised.

Nevertheless, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.

“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said in a statement , adding that Jensen Huang fully backs the review.

After the revelations, Nvidia – whose market capitalisation of $4.5 trillion is higher than the gross domestic product (GDP) of Japan, the world’s fourth-largest economy – saw its stock price tumble by more than 4 percent in trading overnight into Monday.

The controversy erupted as Washington seeks to prevent China from obtaining advanced American semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most powerful artificial intelligence chips, as the US and China fiercely compete for AI supremacy.

So what do we know about the affair, and how will this impact US-China relations and the race for AI dominance?

The allegations first emerged in a New York Times investigation late last month, which reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited by Beijing to gather information about Nvidia’s chief executive and potentially influence the company’s chip sales to China.

However, the precise nature of the information she allegedly obtained, whether any sensitive material was passed to Beijing and how much Jensen Huang knew about the alleged operation remain unclear. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related despite sharing a last name.

The two were reportedly seen together at industry events, including a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology exhibition in 2025.

On Sunday, the Nvidia chief acknowledged his infidelity in a staff memo.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said.

However, in late October, Jensen Huang had told Bloomberg News that his interactions with Alice Huang were related to her company, Megaspeed, describing them as “completely normal and not unusual”.

Also known as Huang Le, Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed International, which provides computing infrastructure used to operate and train AI systems.

According to The New York Times, Megaspeed had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing about $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.

A profile of Alice Huang found in a Chinese investment database listed previous employment at HSBC and Chinese television broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV, according to the AFP news agency, which said it could not independently verify those details.

Alice Huang has not publicly responded to the espionage allegations, and her whereabouts are currently unknown.

Nvidia has launched an independent investigation overseen by a committee of directors and external legal counsel to determine whether its president and CEO was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The company said it had no reason to believe national security or its proprietary information had been compromised while expressing confidence in Jensen Huang’s leadership.

“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” it said, adding that Jensen Huang has pledged to cooperate with the investigation and continue leading the company.

However, the allegations have unsettled investors.

“It deals a blow to the cult of Huang that has taken over the chip world in recent years,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at Britain’s IG Group, a leading derivatives trading firm, told Al Jazeera, while adding that it was too early to determine whether this moment might prove a “major turning point” for Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

“If this turns into a broader congressional investigation, then the shares are likely to come under pressure,” Beauchamp added. “As we learned from the financial crisis [in 2008 and 2009], once you go looking for skeletons in a cupboard, you usually find them.”

Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison, who also works at Nvidia, cancelled a planned visit to South Korea for an Nvidia AI event amid the controversy.

What action has the US government taken?

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over suspicions that the company helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips in violation of US export restrictions.

However, no criminal charges against Jensen Huang or Alice Huang have been reported. The controversy has prompted bipartisan pressure in Washington.

Republican lawmakers on Wednesday called on Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on November 18, arguing that the allegations raise serious questions about China’s potential access to sensitive US technology.

“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” Republican Congressmen John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford said in a statement.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has also demanded answers from Nvidia and called for stronger legislation to prevent advanced US technology from reaching China.

“NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers. And we need to pass bipartisan legislation we have ready to stop advanced American technology from going to China,” she said in a statement.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has defended Jensen Huang, describing him as an “honourable guy”.

Asked whether he should have acted after reportedly receiving an intelligence briefing about the allegations, Trump said, “No, I don’t think so.”

Meanwhile, ⁠⁠⁠⁠Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson ⁠⁠⁠⁠Guo Jiakun on Monday said the “so-called ⁠⁠⁠⁠Chinese spy ⁠⁠⁠⁠narrative” was unsubstantiated. “It is nothing but smears against China,” Guo added.

Jensen Huang, who is seen as a close adviser to Trump on the AI trade , has repeatedly pushed to loosen chip sales restrictions to China.

Can this impact the China-US relationship and the race for AI dominance?

The scandal threatens to intensify tensions between Washington and Beijing over access to the powerful semiconductors needed to develop advanced AI systems. Semiconductors are needed to run nearly all electronics from smartphones to cars and military equipment.

Nvidia is a central player in that competition, supplying chips used by major US technology companies to train and operate AI models. It was until October 30 the most valuable company in the world.

“AI is now a technology that is really shaping national economies and GDPs, and safeguarding becomes even more serious. So protecting not only confidential secrets but also advancements for geopolitical reasons becomes even more important,” Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, told Al Jazeera.

Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China over national security concerns. Nvidia’s top-of-the-line Blackwell GPU chips are banned for export to China.

The US has also clarified that restrictions apply to Chinese-owned companies operating outside China amid concerns that overseas subsidiaries could provide a route around export controls.

However, in December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to China, marking a major easing of US export restrictions. The H200, while not Nvidia’s top chip, is roughly six times more powerful than the model previously approved for sale to China, the H20.

The allegations surrounding Megaspeed could, therefore, increase pressure on Washington to scrutinise Nvidia’s overseas customers and tighten controls on chip shipments.

“Huang has been fairly explicit in his desire to let Nvidia sell to China. That now comes under threat,” Beauchamp said. “We are likely to see the US look to limit exports of the most complex chips, which of course will drive China harder to produce its own versions.”

So far, the US is putting far more private money into AI. In 2025, US private investment in the industry reached $285.9bn, compared with $12.4bn in China, according to Stanford University’s AI Index.

However, Chinese companies have continued developing competitive AI systems despite restrictions on advanced US chips.

In January, the release of the Chinese AI start-up DeepSeek ‘s AI model made headlines after it was built using only a fraction of the money its competitors had spent on their own AI models. Share prices of US tech companies plummeted.

China has advantages in other areas of the AI supply chain, most notably in the production of critical rare earth minerals used in advanced technology. It also generates more than twice as much electricity as the US, giving it access to the vast amounts of relatively cheap power needed to operate AI data centres.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth? Haley Stevens? Hakeem Jeffries faces slew of lame-duck challenges
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is flying high following a midterm landslide that gives Democrats a huge majority next year and makes him a shoo-in for the Speakership. But first, he’s facing some tough choices in the lame-duck session. Congress returns to Washington this week with several high-profile topics on the docket that are…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is flying high following a midterm landslide that gives Democrats a huge majority next year and makes him a shoo-in for the Speakership. But first, he’s facing some tough choices in the lame-duck session.

Congress returns to Washington this week with several high-profile topics on the docket that are likely to divide Democrats and pose challenges for Jeffries and his leadership team just as they’re gearing up to transition into the majority.

The list includes the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which Jeffries has declined to endorse, and permitting reforms governing energy projects that are splitting liberals and centrists within the ideologically diverse caucus.

Jeffries is also facing the tough question of how to approach Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), whose extraordinary, eleventh-hour move to endorse Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race has infuriated many Democrats and led to calls for a disciplinary response.

Jeffries has left open that possibility, saying Stevens made a “terrible decision.” But any such action would highlight Democratic divisions just as the party is working to demonstrate a unified front following its massive election victory. Jeffries punted any decisions to the lame-duck session.

In similar fashion, Democrats are still weighing whether a pair of centrist colleagues, Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), should face repercussions after jumping the aisle to help Republicans advance their messaging agenda ahead of the midterms.

None of those debates rises to the level of the internal strife facing Republicans, whose election drubbing has sparked leadership fights, a rash of finger-pointing, and harsh new questions about the direction of the GOP in the twilight years of the Trump presidency.

Still, each one of those issues will, in its own unique way, pose an early test for Jeffries and his leadership team even as they celebrate their midterm rout.

The question of Hegseth’s fate will likely be the first to arrive. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) moved to force a September vote on eight articles of impeachment against the Defense secretary, half of them related to his handling of the Iran war. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) avoided that preelection vote by calling an early recess, but Massie is promising to revisit the issue as soon as lawmakers return this week.

Hegseth is despised by Democrats, and most appear ready to support Massie’s resolution. But at least some centrist Democrats are likely to oppose the effort. And Jeffries, who will have to work with the administration to get anything done legislatively in the next Congress, has refused to get behind it, saying only that Trump should fire the Pentagon chief.

Asked last week, after the elections, about the Democrats’ approach to Hegseth, Jeffries again leaned on the idea that Trump, not Congress, would deal with him.

“Is Pete Hegseth still around?” Jeffries asked reporters in Washington.

Permitting reform may pose a tougher test. The Senate is poised to vote Monday to advance a bipartisan bill designed to accelerate the approval process for energy and infrastructure projects. Liberals are adamantly opposed to the legislation, warning that it undermines landmark environmental protection laws and threatens the sovereignty of Native American communities.

Jeffries is siding with the liberals, saying he won’t support the package without changes addressing those concerns. But his position is getting pushback from more moderate Democrats, who see the reforms as a key piece of the party’s affordability agenda.

“Modernizing our permitting process is an important way to lower utility costs, create good-paying local jobs, and secure our energy future, and we need to get it done,” Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.) said in a statement, which emphasized that she was breaking from her own leadership.

Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.), who’s expected to lead the New Democrat Coalition in the next Congress, is also gunning to move permitting reform in the lame-duck session.

“This is a truly, I think, an example of a negotiated, bipartisan bill on a very complicated set of issues related to energy and energy generation,” she said last week by phone. “If it gets out of the Senate, I want to be a part of helping to bring it out of the House and get it to the president’s desk.”

The decision surrounding Stevens is much more personal. The Michigan Democrat stunned the country by endorsing Rogers in the final days of the campaign, infuriating Democrats of all stripes. And Curtis Hertel, the head of the Michigan Democratic Party, quickly moved to expel her.

“Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future,” Hertel posted on social platform X.

Some Democrats in the Capitol would like to see a similar punishment. It’s unclear, however, if party leaders want to back such a drastic step, which would highlight internal divisions, especially on the thorny issue of Israel, in a moment that’s been otherwise triumphant. Stevens, who lost in the Senate primary, is not returning to Congress next year, and some Democrats will wonder if it’s worth picking that fight with just a few weeks left in her tenure.

Jeffries has punted the decision, saying he would weigh the options after talking to the broader caucus this week.

“Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic Caucus,” Jeffries said in a statement. “We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return.”

The controversy surrounding Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez has faded amid the focus on the elections. But just two months ago, Democrats were up in arms after the two moderates joined forces with Republicans to pass rules that allowed GOP leaders to advance legislation designed to hurt Democrats in the midterms. Some wanted to strip Gluesenkamp Perez of a plum committee seat. (Golden is retiring and faces less scrutiny.)

Jeffries responded to the outcry by calling a special meeting of the Democrats’ Committee on Caucus Rules to examine potential changes to the party’s internal guidelines heading into the next Congress. The panel left Washington for the long election recess without reaching any conclusions, but members of the committee said they would resume that work in the lame-duck session.

“The process will play out,” Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), a member of the committee, said at the time.

articles.summary: Historic Republican losses on Tuesday have blurred the picture of the party’s presidential field about 15 months before the GOP primaries begin. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), both former presidential candidates, are quickly carving out…
articles.body:
Historic Republican losses on Tuesday have blurred the picture of the party’s presidential field about 15 months before the GOP primaries begin.

Vice President Vance’s path to succeeding President Trump has become rockier, while figures including outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), both former presidential candidates, are quickly carving out a postmidterm path of their own.

And there’s no shortage of high-profile Republicans who could jump in as the party searches for a new torchbearer. Here’s the top five contenders — for now:

Vance, 42, still has the inside track to the Republican nomination, but his intimate role in the White House midterm campaign looks like a liability.

The vice president now faces the daunting challenge of being a part of an increasingly unpopular administration, while trying to convince voters he represents some kind of change.

“It’s the MAGA base that’s still the decider of the presidential nominees, and Vance is still probably the best embodiment of the MAGA base, but you know he also has to own every decision that is made the past two years and the next year,” Arizona-based GOP strategist Barrett Marson said.

Vance has proven an adept, if adaptable, political messenger. He was a sharp critic of Trump before running for Senate in Ohio and then joining his 2024 ticket. And after the midterms, Vance quickly pinned the blame on the war Trump started more than eight months ago.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy social media post. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

Trump said he thought Vance’s statement was “good” but continued to dodge questions about whether he would endorse Vance for 2028.

“Maybe you have a lot of people running. Maybe nobody’s going to run. Maybe he won’t run. I don’t know who’s going to run,” Trump told reporters Wednesday.

Vance is close to Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr. The vice president himself has said he is undecided about running and hasn’t spoken to President Trump about a 2028 campaign.

One national political consultant involved in competitive races suggested Vance may be thinking about whether to run at all, given the postmidterm environment.

“I think Vance is no fool,” the consultant said. “He’s probably asking, ‘Am I going to commit the next two years of this when the odds of success are pretty slim?’”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is seen as the most likely presidential candidate within Trump’s Cabinet. The State Department denied reports this week that he’s considering stepping down to prepare for a presidential run.

Rubio, 55, won his Florida Senate seat in 2010; the seat will be occupied by Sen. Ashley Moody (R) for the next six years. Rubio ran against Trump for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination.

While Vance remains the favorite in betting markets and Republican straw polls, Rubio fares better in hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates, according to a survey taken by Emerson College and The Hill back in August.

Like Vance, Rubio was critical of Trump before becoming a close ally. Rubio, who is also the national security adviser, is seen as a driving force in Trump’s operations in Venezuela: removing Nicolás Maduro and transforming relations with his former government.

As a son of Cuban immigrants, he has long said he wants to bring regime change to Cuba as well.

Rubio hasn’t said anything publicly about Tuesday’s midterm election results. He mostly kept his distance from Trump’s midterm campaign, though in the homestretch he was pulled onto the stage and spoke for 11 seconds.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.), who won his reelection Tuesday, told Fox News Digital that he was throwing his support behind Rubio following the GOP’s midterm performance.

Tim Chapman, president of former Vice President Mike Pence’s Advancing American Freedom, said “one thing Rubio has going for him is that he does have just instinctively coalitional capabilities.”

The consultant said, “I agree that Rubio is a much stronger candidate than Vance. But I think Rubio is again asking, ‘What’s the nomination worth?’”

DeSantis has been very public since the midterms, despite not being on the ticket himself.

The term-limited governor has placed blame squarely on Trump for Tuesday’s disaster. He called the midterm outcome an “extinction-level event” for Republicans. He said the results are “no question … a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over.”

DeSantis ran against Trump for the GOP presidential nomination in 2024 and was an early favorite before Trump shored up party support. The 48-year-old looks like a rare GOP winner from the midterms, with Florida maintaining its red status as other states like Texas and Kansas flipped blue.

Marson said DeSantis has a potentially convincing case.

“Ron DeSantis is trying to repeat his moment from four years ago, and this time it actually could stick, because he gets to point to a lot of great things in Florida, including one of the only red states that actually remained red,” he said.

Chapman predicted DeSantis will “become much more critical of some of the excesses of the second Trump term.”

Cruz is the most likely senator to throw his hat in the ring, but he may not be the only one. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) are seen as having bigger ambitions, though Hawley said recently he had “no intention” of running.

Cruz hasn’t ruled out another presidential run. He’s up for reelection to his Senate seat in 2030. Like Rubio, Cruz was a Trump rival in the 2016 presidential race before backing the president in the years since.

He said the midterm loss to Democrats was a “blue tsunami” and an “a– kicking.”

“Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas,” Cruz said on his podcast. “In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election.”

Vance said last month it’s “really obvious” that Cruz is running for president. Cruz said in an August MS NOW interview that Vance does not automatically have the 2028 GOP nomination and that he wants to “certainly be part of the discussion.”

Speaking with Politico in September, he said the party needs to question whether it’s a “small-government, free-market conservative party” or a “big-government, nanny-state party.”

He also said he thinks there’s a divide over the party’s foreign policy, one centered on whether the GOP is an “isolationist party that wants to withdraw from the world” or one that believes “in American leadership in the world.”

Chapman said Cruz is “clearly making a play for the free market wing of the party.”

Former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, 59, is among a handful of current and former governors who might see a more moderate path to the presidency. Georgia’s outgoing governor, Brian Kemp, is another.

Youngkin served as Virginia’s governor from 2022 to 2026. He has sidestepped questions about his political future but praised Vance earlier this year, saying he would be a “great nominee.”

In August, Youngkin founded a national policy group that promotes school choice, called Empowering America’s Parents. He told Bloomberg in August that he’s been asked about running for president many times.

“I’ve answered it the same way every time, which is I don’t anticipate being on the debate stage,” he said.

During his time as governor, the multimillionaire investor put a focus on education reform, parental rights and economic growth. He also vetoed a bill in 2025 that would have imposed more regulations on data centers, an industry that proved very unpopular in state elections.

Marson described Youngkin as a “national darling” but noted that maybe “his time has passed.”

The consultant described Youngkin as “a Christian Mitt Romney.”

“The party may get back to that someday, but it’s certainly not ready for a Glenn Youngkin today,” the consultant said. “That’s fine for a governor in a purple-slash-blue state, but I just don’t see how that appeals to primary voters.”

articles.title: Why a midterm blue wave could doom the college sports bill
articles.summary: A dominant performance by Democrats in last week’s midterm elections is expected to severely slow the progress of — if not entirely kill off — congressional efforts to regulate the big business of college sports. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to become the first Black Speaker in January, has backed the…
articles.body:
A dominant performance by Democrats in last week’s midterm elections is expected to severely slow the progress of — if not entirely kill off — congressional efforts to regulate the big business of college sports.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to become the first Black Speaker in January, has backed the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) and NAACP in opposing the bill and other NCAA-backed proposals like it in recent months.

Jeffries will replace outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who this past week said he would not stay on as House minority leader. Johnson is a key member of the president’s “Saving College Sports” White House task force.

Johnson faces a slew of other priorities in the lame-duck Congress, including government spending and an authorization of defense funds.

He’s also likely to be dealing with a shortage of votes, as it can be difficult to ensure attendance in lame-duck sessions when many members, defeated at the ballot box, are not motivated to be in Washington. That could be a factor with a GOP conference that is losing dozens of members and that had a narrow majority in the first place.

The college sports bill, most Capitol Hill observers agree, is likely to fall to the back burner during the final House session of the calendar year given those changes.

“There is still a path, but I think the window is closing quickly. The Senate’s bipartisan vote was a major accomplishment, but the House has its own priorities and concerns,” said Christopher Pham, a sports business and finance attorney who has been closely tracking the legislation’s progress. “With a compressed legislative calendar and a change in congressional control approaching, I think the odds are against the bill getting across the finish line this session.”

Pham was referring to the Senate’s vote to pass college sports legislation before the fall recess despite strong opposition from Senate Democrats and questions about the bill’s viability in the House.

The legislation, which is backed by President Trump and major conferences like the SEC and Big Ten, would grant the NCAA a key antirust protection shielding it from litigation around the enforcement of its rules on eligibility, the transfer portal and name, image and likeness (NIL) money paid to student athletes.

It caps NIL spending by NCAA member schools and sets a national standard on health benefits provided to student-athletes. It would also create a framework for revenue sharing within athletic departments to keep women’s and Olympic sports healthy.

The bill’s critics, including the CBC and the NAACP, contend it would unfairly limit the earning potential of minority athletes and disproportionately harm nonwhite students while protecting the salaries of coaches and administrators.

Jeffries and the CBC in May called on top high school recruits in the South to boycott SEC schools over what they contend is racially motivated gerrymandering in Southern states.

SEC schools would benefit in a big way from the Protect College Sports Act’s (PCSA) passage, and Congress should not protect a system that exploits minority athletes, they argue.

“If the SEC schools are for this bill, we are against it,” Jeffries told reporters outside the Capitol, calling efforts to send a message about fairness and compensation to the NCAA and its backers a “Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson moment” for student-athletes.

Johnson’s team tried and failed last year to pass the Student Compensation and Opportunity through Rights and Endorsements (SCORE) Act, a similar proposal backed by the NCAA.

Johnson had before Tuesday’s midterms told reporters he believes his party can whip enough support for the bill after the recess, but now questions loom.

In recent weeks, some House lawmakers have said they are concerned the bill does not do enough to alleviate questions about a host of issues ranging from game integrity relating to online wagering to punishments for poor officiating in college football specifically.

Others are uncomfortable with how much certain states, like Texas and Alabama, would benefit from the PCSA compared with smaller schools outside the SEC and Big Ten.

“It’s big business, and now you go throwing in the millions of dollars involved with the agents and coaches and online gambling, there’s all these different exploitations that are taking place,” Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Fla.) told The Hill during a recent interview. “As much as I appreciate the work Ted Cruz has done on this thing, I still question his motives on coveting this bill because I know how the rest of the Texas delegation feels, why would he feel any different?”

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who led the Senate effort to get the PCSA passed, has argued the legislation should be at the top of the House’s agenda this week.

Cruz had hoped to secure a political win from Trump, who he suggested should sign the legislation live on ESPN’s “College GameDay.” After Tuesday’s blue wave, the chances of such a made for television spectacle playing out look increasingly slim.

“The reality is Democrats have other priorities, which makes this incredibly unlikely to make it out of the lame duck,” said Matt Cowan, an attorney who has represented several NCAA schools fighting litigation on issues like NIL and revenue sharing.

“We’re still optimistic that there is some version of a bill that can be passed. From what we’ve seen from the last best version of the Senate [bill] is ‘we’re done here; we’re not going back to the drawing board.’”

Major sports figures saw mixed results in last week’s midterm elections. The GOP’s lone victory came from former New York Yankee slugger Mark Teixeira, who won a U.S. House seat in Texas, while former NFL kicker Jay Feely lost his bid to join the lower chamber in Arizona. Former sports reporter Michele Tafoya also lost her race for Minnesota Senate, while Democrat Josh Turek, a Paralympic and former professional basketball player, rode a blue wave to a Senate seat in Iowa. Former Auburn University football coach and Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville also won a spot in the Alabama governor’s mansion as expected.

A motion hearing is set for Friday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., in the widely followed case involving President Trump’s planned takeover of East Potomac Golf Links. Judge Ana Reyes is expected to press government lawyers over the administration’s plans for the Hains Point property after accusing the Department of Justice of misleading her about Trump’s desire to redevelop the location last week. The hearing comes just two days before what the president says will be East Potomac’s final day of operation on Nov. 15, a shuttering that would defy an order by Reyes barring future work at the property while the case is being litigated.

The chances of a MLB lockout looked increasingly likely as the calendar turned to November. During recent negotiations, league owners proposed punting on a salary cap until 2028 and shortening the season to 154 games. The MLB players union has so far rejected those concessions and accused the league of operating in bad faith. Some observers have predicted labor regulators from President Trump’s administration could ultimately get involved as a mediator before or after the current collective bargaining agreement expires at midnight on Dec. 1.

Jocks on the Hill: Del. James Moylan (R-Guam)

Del. James Moylan (R-Guam), who last week lost a reelection bid to represent the U.S. territory of Guam in Congress, answered some sports questions earlier this summer for The Hill.

“Ya know it’s so boring because it’s the only sport I ever played … bowling! I really enjoy it.”

“See in Guam we don’t really do that, we don’t have those teams, which is part of the reason politics is so important to us. But I will say … Taylor Swift is my favorite football team.”

Is there an athlete you really admired growing up?

“Well, it changed a lot but I love Joe Namath. He was great. A quarterback for the Jets a long time ago but man, he was cool.”

Hate is a strong word but is there a team you love to root against?

Is there a sports or politics cliche that resonates with you?

“What do you call those guys that are sitting on the couch watching the game and they’re giving all the calls and telling the teams what they’re doing wrong … armchair quarterbacks. We got a lot of those folks in the news media against us. Everybody knows how to do it better than politicians, but they’re not the ones inside.”

ESPN’s Michael A. Fletcher published an interesting story examining the impact of Florida’s Teddy Bridgewater Act signed this summer, which allows high school coaches to pay up to $15,000 in expenses for student-athletes. In some cases, Fletcher writes, for a student-athlete “a full stomach depends on a coach’s wallet.”

The Athletic’s Chad Graff has a great profile of Rob Gronkowski , who was inducted into the New England Patriots Hall of Fame over the weekend. It’s chock-full of entertaining quotes, nuggets and stories from players and coaches who know him best.

Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international competition last week, so Sports Illustrated put together a nostalgic list of the star forward’s most memorable moments.

articles.title: The next generation of workers is taking its talent and spending power to this Southern state
articles.summary: South Carolina posted the largest net gain of Gen Z adults through interstate migration in 2024, but California lost more than 58,000 young residents.
articles.body: The next generation of workers is on the move, and South Carolina is drawing more young adults than any other state. The Palmetto State recorded a net gain of 22,843 Gen Z adults through interstate migration in 2024, according to a new LendingTree analysis. The study defines Gen Z as adults ages 18 to 27, the generation that follows millennials. LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst Matt Schulz told Fox News Digital that affordability and job prospects may help explain the state’s appeal. South Carolina’s proximity to Charlotte, he said, gives young adults access to a growing job market while potentially offering a less expensive place to live. "Gen Z is at the most mobile time of their lives, and they’re looking for a place where they can live affordably, where there are decent jobs and good opportunity," Schulz said. RED STATES HAVE SPENT DECADES DOMINATING A KEY CORNER OF THE ECONOMY California had the largest net loss of Gen Z residents, at 58,109. Texas was the most popular destination for those leaving, drawing 19,287 Californians. Schulz said California, New Jersey and New York had some of the largest net losses, while South Carolina, Missouri, Tennessee and Texas posted net gains. But he said young adults are also looking for career opportunities and a lifestyle they can afford. "Ultimately, it is about looking for job opportunity and looking for the best place to get started with your career and being able to afford the things that you want to do and have the life you want to live," he said. AMERICANS KEEP MOVING TO TEXAS AND FLORIDA — BUT ONE OTHER RED STATE IS GROWING EVEN FASTER The figures build on a broader migration trend. South Carolina added more than 59,000 residents from other states between 2022 and 2023, gaining roughly $4.1 billion in income, according to IRS data cited in an earlier Fox News Digital analysis. The state had the nation’s largest per-capita net gain, while Texas and Florida drew more newcomers overall. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Schulz said young adults’ moves can have broader economic implications as they enter the workforce, start families and make major purchases. "These are the future leaders of your country and the future business owners and parents," he said. "The future of our economy depends a lot on what Gen Z does, whether it’s the housing market or auto loans or starting small businesses."

articles.title: ‘Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?’: In a nail-biter Senate race, the incumbent stays out of view in Mississippi
articles.summary: As the Mississippi Senate race still remains too close to call, Democrat Scott Colom and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith have taken completely different approaches...
articles.body:
As the Mississippi Senate race still remains too close to call, Democrat Scott Colom and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith have taken completely different approaches towards the public.

Since Election Day, Colom has held at least eight events and capitalized on the national attention of the race to flood the airwaves and make his case for why Democrats should no longer count out a state historically considered a Republican stronghold. Meanwhile, Hyde-Smith has not been seen publicly since she left her election night watch party just outside of Jackson after declaring that she would remain her state's junior senator.

While Colom has appeared at local universities, a Black-owned bookshop, a vinyl record store, a diner, and a senior citizens center and sat for multiple interviews with the media, Hyde-Smith has made her statements solely on X, including posting a Bible verse about hope on Sunday.

"Ultimately, at some point, the senator needs to speak out. Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?" Colom told reporters on Friday at the senior citizens facility in Jackson. "We want to hear from her. She needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn't have one."

Hyde-Smith's campaign manager Jake Monssen said in a statement to CNN, "Senator Hyde-Smith and our team are working around the clock across Mississippi to protect the integrity of this election and to ensure every legal vote is counted."

Hyde-Smith is expected to appear in Washington on Monday as the Senate returns to session after a six-week recess.

The divergent strategies speak to a dynamic that played out across the country this election cycle where Republicans in GOP strongholds like Hyde-Smith, who did not work to get ahead of the worsening national political landscape, were caught flatfooted and now find themselves in a once-unthinkable position.

Now, Colom leads the incumbent senator by 2,500 votes in a race that could come down to thousands of provisional ballots, which election officials will vet in the coming days. If he wins, he will be Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator since the Reconstruction era.

Hyde-Smith's campaign refused Colom's invitations to debate prior to Election Day and did relatively few campaign events even as Colom was frequently on the trail and appearing with top Democrats like Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton.

Even some of Hyde-Smith's supporters have noticed their senator's absence and how Colom has filled that void.

John, an insurance adjuster from Hyde-Smith's hometown of Brookhaven who declined to disclose his last name, is disappointed the Republican senator did not win in a landslide. Describing his community as the buckle to the Bible Belt, a county where Hyde-Smith outperformed Colom nearly 2:1, it's hard for him to picture his home state turning blue. But John said he wished Hyde-Smith matched the television ads that he was inundated by from the Colom campaign.

"I would like to personally have seen more campaigning from Cindy," he told CNN. "I would like to have seen more ads for Cindy and put her name out there a little more. And it may be because she's an incumbent and maybe didn't feel like the need was there. I'm not sure. I don't know."

For F.B. Warren, who has served on school boards with Hyde-Smith, Colom's campaign should be a wakeup call for Republicans about how to not take Mississippi for granted.

"It's kind of like the team that plays a game of football, baseball, basketball, and they never have competition," Warren told CNN. "So, in Mississippi and across the country, from the Republican Party standpoint, they got pushed. They now got pushed, so they're going to have to get better. They're going to have to campaign better. They're going to have to have better candidates. They're going to have to work harder, and that's the big wake-up call."

His wife, Angie Warren, who owns two small stores in Hyde-Smith's hometown, reflected on how Democrats did more to capitalize on voter enthusiasm this election season.

"I do think that the Democratic Party has a better turnout for elections than the Republican Party. I don't know why that is. I don't know if they speak closer to the people and they get out and vote more. But for some reason, the Republican Party doesn't always have the voter turnout that it needs," she told CNN.

While Mississippi has long been Republican territory, Colom and other Democrats have argued that the headwinds against the party in power and the state's significant Black electorate made the state fertile ground for a flip this cycle. Further, Hyde-Smith, who was first appointed to the Senate in 2018, underperformed Republicans in 2020 as well, winning a full term by 10 points even as Trump won the state by 16.

The early lack of national attention to the race gave Colom a long runway to capitalize on Hyde-Smith's uneven campaign performance.

It wasn't until late October that the Senate Leadership Fund, the leading GOP super PAC focused on Senate races, made an initial reservation of about $160,000 in Mississippi, according to AdImpact data. That reservation was in response to Senate Democrats announcing that they would spend r oughly $1 million on ads for the race. By that time, Colom had started to galvanize the party behind what was once considered a long-shot bid in a state Trump won two years ago by 23 points.

Hyde-Smith has posted on social media since Election Day, including a statement on November 6 stating, "we are not backing down. This election is not over" and vowing to "see this through to the very end!"

Mississippi GOP Chair Michael Hurst held a press conference last week to tout the 50-plus volunteer attorneys and observers Republicans had sent across the state, with many more are prepared to jump in to help.

"Our attorneys and observers will continue to be in different parts of Mississippi – watching as election commissioners review and process these outstanding ballots, ensuring that our elections are followed and that only ballots which have been legally cast are counted," he said.

Even as both sides prepare for a potential legal battle over the results, Democrat Phillip Rollins told CNN that Colom's nonstop style channeled the frustration that he and others were feeling in the lead up to the election.

"People are fed up," Rollins, who owns the comic book and record shop where Colom recently campaigned, said. "They need to see the change happen during their lifetime and not have to wait."

articles.title: Senate Republicans return to Capitol furious with Trump after big losses
articles.summary: Senate Republicans returning to the Capitol on Monday are furious with President Trump, whom they blame for last week’s big losses in Senate and House races. The anger is raising the chances that the party could pivot away from the lame-duck president in the lead-up to the 2028 presidential election, according to GOP aides and…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans returning to the Capitol on Monday are furious with President Trump, whom they blame for last week’s big losses in Senate and House races.

The anger is raising the chances that the party could pivot away from the lame-duck president in the lead-up to the 2028 presidential election, according to GOP aides and strategists.

Tensions are also rising with Trump’s Friday announcement that immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller will be his new chief of staff, replacing the outgoing Susie Wiles.

The Miller appointment suggests a doubling down on the president’s policies, particularly on immigration enforcement, after an election in which Hispanic voters swung decisively toward Democrats, especially in Texas.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday said Miller should be fired, not promoted.

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman said in an interview on CNN. “You don’t promote those who are — who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered.”

Whit Ayres, a prominent Republican pollster, said Senate Republicans will be less deferential to Trump after suffering a huge loss of seats in last week’s election.

Ayres said Trump “clearly will remain the leader of the party for the next two years, but I also think the knee-jerk obeisance to whatever his whims are at the moment is likely over.”

“There is so much resentment particularly among Republicans in the Senate for what Donald Trump did in North Carolina and South Carolina and Texas,” he said, referring to Trump’s endorsement of candidates Michael Whatley, Darline Graham and Ken Paxton, who all lost by large margins in the general election.

“I think his iron grip over the Senate Republicans is likely to be loosened,” Ayres said.

One senior Senate Republican aide predicted GOP senators and the broader party will begin to shift away from Trump over the next year.

“Trump said he was on the ballot. He wasn’t on the ballot but acted like he was on the ballot,” and “a lot of people” voted as if Trump was atop the GOP ticket when they voted for Democrats in battleground states around the country, the aide said.

“We need somebody who can work together with people, who doesn’t just try to divide — who is focused on real issues that people care about that are of importance versus stupid little internet memes, which it seems like Trump and Vance are more focused on now,” the aide argued.

Republican sources say Trump undermined their chances of winning key Senate races by endorsing weak candidates, such as Paxton and Graham, and by failing to adhere to any message discipline.

GOP senators are also frustrated by what they saw as Trump’s reluctance to spend from his massive campaign war chest until late in the campaign.

Senate Republican aides and pollsters say Trump’s dismal influence on races across the country will spark an intense discussion about what’s next for the party and whether it’s time to turn the page on MAGA and its policies.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and members of his leadership team lobbied Trump for months to back Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) over Paxton, the state attorney general, in the Texas Senate Republican primary — or to at least stay neutral — but Trump ignored their advice and endorsed Paxton before the primary runoff, sinking Cornyn’s chances.

Thune and his leadership team urged the president and Senate GOP colleagues to keep their political messaging focused on their legislative accomplishments, especially the popular tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, such as its tax deductions for tips.

But Trump instead often veered off from the plan, getting into fights over the White House ballroom, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the Kennedy Center, the East Potomac Park golf course and other topics that GOP strategists viewed as unhelpful to delivering the broader Republican message.

Trump blamed last week’s losses on poor Republican candidates, but many Senate Republicans think the blame for the loss of at least seven seats lies squarely with the unpopular president.

“We’re up here talking about the generational benefits of avoiding a $4 trillion-plus tax hike and everything else that’s inside that bill, and then the president is talking about the Reflecting Pool or the ballroom, and those are the things that get the headlines,” a Senate GOP aide said. “Message synchronization was off.”

Senate Republicans were galled when Trump dismissed the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act as a “big yawn.”

GOP leaders were touting the bipartisan legislation as a major accomplishment to address housing affordability, but Trump popped their balloon as he said he cared more about passing the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a package to overhaul election rules that had virtually no chance of passing Congress.

Senate Republican sources also said Trump waited too long to spend the hundreds of millions of dollars he stockpiled ahead of the midterm elections.

“They sat on that $400 million until it was too late to start spending it,” a second GOP aide said.

Trump said in August he would spend “a lot” of money from a pro-Trump super PAC to help “good” GOP candidates, but Senate GOP strategists complained the president’s political allies waited until the final weeks of the campaign to dump money into races, which diluted their firepower because they had to pay higher television ad rates.

Trump announced in late October that he would end up spending more than $400 million by Election Day to help Republicans keep Congress.

When Republicans got blown out on Election Day, the White House blamed GOP candidates for not putting in as much effort as the president to promote their candidacies and records.

Trump declared on election night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Senate Republicans say they think Trump also hurt them by constantly bashing their failure to pass the SAVE America Act, even after Republicans held at least five votes on the legislation, either in whole or in part, and came nowhere close to collecting the 60 votes the bill needed to advance.

Trump warned Senate Republicans would be “in big trouble” if they didn’t abolish the filibuster to ram the bill through the chamber.

“When you’re casting your own teammate as the opponent, what message does that send to the voter?” the GOP aide said.

A third Senate Republican aide argued that Trump clearly deserves the blame for the loss of seven — and maybe as many as nine — Senate seats and more than 40 House seats.

“Trump’s message was, ‘I’m going to deliver you a good economy,’ and it seems like the only person who benefited from the economy was him,” the aide said, adding that Democrats successfully tied together voters’ concerns about rising prices and corruption in Washington.

“Those two things led to a disaster with independents,” the aide said.

The GOP aide said some Senate Republicans expect more “pushback to Trump because his half-life is rapidly diminishing” but cautioned that “he’s still a popular figure in the Republican Party.”

The president’s elevation of Miller, who is seen as a conservative hard-liner, may be a bid to keep base MAGA voters firmly in his corner.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), one of Miller’s sharpest critics in the Senate GOP conference, called his elevation to chief of staff a “colossal mistake.”

“The worst of all possible choices,” Tillis told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “The president needs to rethink it.”

Senate Republican candidate John Sununu blamed Trump for his double-digit loss to Rep. Chris Pappas (D) in New Hampshire, a state that Senate GOP leaders in August saw as a promising opportunity to flip a Democratic-held seat.

Sununu said Trump’s failure to end the months-long conflict with Iran and a steady stream of media stories about Trump’s family business dealings sunk his chances of winning.

“This president ran and won on a platform of no more needless, endless wars. And then he attacked Iran, and we’re still in it,” he told SiriusXM’s “The John Kasich Show.”

“This president ran on and won on a platform of drain the swamp, right? … And now it seems like he or his family is in on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” he said. “And those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can’t vote for a Republican while he’s still in office.’”

Cornyn argued Trump “misread his mandate” after the 2024 election.

He argued the president’s “arbitrary” decisions on tariffs raised prices for millions of Americans without improving trade deals, and the administration’s “hyperaggressive” immigration enforcement efforts went well beyond what voters expected.

“Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring. Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement,” Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed.

Other Republicans have stepped up to defend Thune and Senate GOP leaders, arguing that they had little control over the negative political environment that Trump played a major role in creating.

“I don’t think any rational, honest person … could blame John Thune for any of this,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) told reporters shortly before the election. “I don’t think anybody could blame him for any bad outcome.”

Asked if Trump would get most of the blame if Republicans lost control of the Senate, Cramer only said, “There will be a lot of finger-pointing.”

articles.title: They left no doubt: There’s a bright side for everyone about the midterm result
articles.summary: Both sides spent the weeks before the midterms undermining faith in the elections, but the outcome left no room for doubt.
articles.body:
If you’re a Democrat, then you’re pretty happy with the outcome of last week’s election. If you’re a Republican, then you just had a very rough week.

But if you’re a small-c conservative dedicated to the health of the republic, it was not a total disaster. There were silver linings, and I’m not talking only about the ending of certain slimy Republican candidates’ careers — think Vivek Ramaswamy and Ken Paxton.

No, I’m talking about the size and scope of the Democratic victories, particularly in the Senate races, which were thorough and decisive across the board. The silver lining is not merely that serious Democratic contenders thumped Republican joke candidates in states such as South Carolina and Texas, but the margins by which they won — victories so complete as to forestall another round of civic trust-eroding “stolen election” conspiracy theories.

And thank goodness for those margins, because both sides were clearly itching to allege all manner of fraud and treachery for any closely contested race. They spent the weeks leading up to the elections laying the groundwork for such messaging campaigns.

On the right, President Trump and his influencer goons spread the usual conspiracy theories — the familiar winking and grinning at questions about the reliability of election results. There were also concrete steps, including the Justice Department sending federal employees to polling centers in places such as Utah, with limited advance notice and little coordination with state officials .

On the left, Democratic officials spread their own flavor of doubt and paranoia. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said there was “ no question ” in his mind that the Justice Department would “try to steal this election.” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Republicans would try “ any diabolical scheme to prevent Nov. 3 from being a free and fair election .” Various characters began promoting a conspiracy theory about a rogue Republican House clerk refusing to seat the new majority , something no one is talking about now and was always highly unlikely .

In the middle, the national press primed the pump of election-trutherism with weeks of irresponsible “stolen election” scaremongering. No conspiracy theory was too small, no unfounded suspicion too stupid to elevate and grant a veneer of legitimacy.

“Nine ways the Trump administration could interfere with the midterms,” Reuters warned.

Newsweek ran a speculative headline: “How Trump Could Interfere With the Midterms on Election Day, and the Days After.”

The New York Times asked: “If Democrats Win Congress, Could the G.O.P. Refuse to Seat Them?”

On election night, November 3, before all the races had been called, Trump told the New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept those results,” adding, “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”

That was as welcome as the victory margins themselves.

It is a blessing that Democratic Senate candidates Roy Cooper, James Talarico, and Troy Jackson, won their races by 19, 12, and six points, respectively. No late-night tally updates, recounts, boxes of absentee ballots discovered in car-trunks or disputed totals in those races. The victories left no question about who won. They left little opportunity for frauds, opportunists or cranks to stoke further doubt. (There is still time for “stolen election” claims in the unfinished Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi, but control of Congress is already decided, so the stakes are much lower.)

The election cycle could not have come at a better time.

Waning faith in elections is a bipartisan problem. Trump has sown doubt among the Republican base, as a sacked U.S. Capitol and the state of Georgia can attest. Democrats have also undermined their base’s confidence, and the polling shows it: Forty-one percent of Kamala Harris voters believe Trump did not legitimately win a second term; the share of Democrats who believe votes will be counted accurately in U.S. elections fell from 75 percent in 2022 to 55 percent in 2026 . Democrats who say they are “confident mail and absentee votes will be counted as voters intend” dropped from 88 percent in 2022 to 64 percent this year ; and 72 percent of Democratic respondents said ahead of the midterms that the elections would be “well-run,” down from a peak of 90 percent in 2024.

Although the 2026 midterms will not put every concern to rest, they at least did not further damage faith in the process. In fact, one can reasonably argue that, if anything, last week’s clear outcomes will help restore some confidence — not only for Democrats, but for Republicans as well.

As for those small-c conservatives, including those of the social variety, they can also take some satisfaction from the successful passage of statewide ballot measures that limited the power of government, including in North Carolina and Wisconsin , along with measures requiring voter ID and barring males from playing in women’s and girls’ sports .

In fact, for the conservative, one potential takeaway from the midterms is that voters emphatically do not like the Trump Republican Party’s “anything goes” style of politics, but neither are they clamoring for far-left governance.

There is no reason to think everything will calm down — that this is the end to the political chaos that has marked the last 11 years. After all, a second-term lame-duck president with an addiction to executive orders has little to fear in the way of political consequences.

For now, though, the midterms did not add to the already unsettling number of people who doubt whether elections are as free and fair as advertised. If you are a Democrat, you are already happy. But if you are a small-government conservative who cares about the long-term trajectory of the country and civic comity, then that is also something to be thankful for, even if some radical Democrats won office.

It is not a major victory, but it is a silver lining.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.
