articles.title: Rubio defends Trump's Iran war as not 'necessarily popular, but necessary'
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's Iran war as "necessary" to prevent a nuclear weapon, even as he ties it to Republican midterm losses.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended President Donald Trump's decision to launch the war on Iran, saying it was "necessary" to prevent Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Rubio admitted that the war was not "necessarily popular," acknowledging the war's impact on the Republicans' midterm election losses last week. Rubio made the statement in response to questions about Vice President JD Vance's statement last week that also pinned the losses on the war. Rubio said Trump was responding to a "very real threat" when he launched the war earlier this year. VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' "He addressed it even though oftentimes the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary," Rubio said. Trump himself has made no apologies for the war, stating repeatedly since Election Day that he had no choice but to intervene in Iran's nuclear program. TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES "I can tell you if I had it to do again, this historically — for history — will go down as one of the best things we ever did," Trump told reporters on Sunday. "Because if they ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world." Trump nevertheless told "60 Minutes" in an interview this weekend that he is not currently looking to escalate the conflict. IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES The U.S. and Iran are engaged in talks, but Rubio says they are making little progress. "I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough," Rubio said. "Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic." TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION Iran lifted its self-imposed ballistic missile-range limit and threatened to unleash new, homegrown weapons on Sunday within hours of the U.S. military launching a new task force aimed at choking off Tehran's weapons shipments and illicit trade on Nov. 7. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi confirmed that Iran was now abandoning its previous 2,000-kilometer, or roughly 1,240-mile, ballistic missile-range restriction. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That restriction has been lifted for us," Mohebbi clarified in the wake of the task force announcement. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Stephen Miller era begins in Trump’s White House
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Congress returns for lame duck ▪ Votes trickle in Mississippi, Alaska ▪ Dana White meeting about press secretary offer ▪ Eisenkot gets chance to form government A new chapter starts today in the White House as hard-liner Stephen Miller takes over as President Trump‘s chief of staff in the aftermath of the…
articles.body:
▪ Dana White meeting about press secretary offer

▪ Eisenkot gets chance to form government

A new chapter starts today in the White House as hard-liner Stephen Miller takes over as President Trump ‘s chief of staff in the aftermath of the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses.

Having served as the deputy chief of staff for policy, Miller has arguably been a driving force behind strict immigration enforcement policies, including the deadly crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Now, he’s taking over for the much less vocal Susie Wiles , who seemed comfortable working as a behind-the-scenes operator for the past two years. Miller’s appointment has been widely perceived as a message that the White House is preparing for combat with the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress.

However, Trump said he’s hoping to be able to work with Democrats during a sit-down interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday. One of the key areas he pointed to was immigration — the issue that Miller has for years known to be a hard-liner on.

Trump said he believes his administration’s deportation policy was “too tough.” He noted the argument that those who entered the country illegally who have jobs and are paying taxes should be allowed to stay in the U.S. in some form.

“The deal would be we would work something out, and I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” Trump said.

Following the GOP’s losses last Tuesday, Trump surprised some with a congratulatory message to Democrats, saying he looks forward to working together “for the good of our country.”

But The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports many political observers see Miller’s promotion as a clear signal that Trump has no intention of backing down.

“They are not going to slow down on executive power, executive orders, and regulations,” Joe Grogan , the former director of Trump’s Domestic Policy Council in his first administration, told Manchester. “Stephen is going to move aggressively on all of that.”

Democrats have widely slammed Miller’s promotion, saying it undermines the possibility of working together with the president.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said Friday in a post on the social platform X that Miller becoming the chief of staff shows Trump has “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” Schumer said. “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) called Miller the “most broken man.”

“I don’t know what Stephen Miller has actually contributed to our culture, our society, in any real way, except to make us more angry and stoke the worst kind of fear and vitriol,” he said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.”

Even some Republicans expressed concern about Miller.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) called Miller’s promotion a “bad mistake” during an interview Sunday with CNN’s Manu Raju .

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people. You don’t promote those who are, who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered,” he said, adding that Midwesterners don’t like his “tone.”

Wiles, who was the first-ever female White House chief of staff, is one of the first in what is likely to be a growing list of administration figures exiting after the bruising midterms.

Deputy chief of staff Richard Walters , a close ally of Wiles, is also leaving the administration .

▪ The Hill : Bernie Sanders ‘not worried’ about Miller.

▪ The Hill : Katie Miller pauses podcast after husband’s promotion.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced it’s opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang following reports that he had an intimate relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China . The company’s stock is set to drop when trading opens on Monday.

Trump said he’s “highly unlikely” to attack Iran if upcoming peace talks yield progress on Tehran’s nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He told CNN that he believes Iran wants to make a deal. Trump previously ruled out striking Iran before the midterms happened.

World leaders will gather on Monday in Antalya, Turkey for the U.N. climate summit, called COP31. Delegates will face pressure to negotiate new pledges but also make good on past commitments meant to slow the rise in global average temperatures.

The Capitol is seen under gray skies after American voters this week flipped control of both chambers of Congress from Republican control to the Democrats, in Washington, on Nov. 6, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite, Associated Press)

BACK IN TOWN : The House and Senate are returning to Washington today after weeks away ahead of last week’s elections, facing a packed agenda for the lame-duck session.

The most high-profile item for this week is deciding who will lead House Republicans in the next session of Congress.

With Speaker Mike Johnson (La.) not seeking the role, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.) is facing off against House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (Ohio). The vote, scheduled for Tuesday.

Some members argue a total revamp of leadership is needed, while others say Scalise is better positioned for the top spot. Contested elections for minority whip and conference chair are also taking place.

At the same time, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Democrats are widely expected to support it. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said he’s a “hard yes” on the resolution in an interview on Sunday.

And the clock is ticking for lawmakers to make progress on extending government funding before it runs out on Dec. 11.

Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi here on what to expect as Congress returns.

▪ The Hill : Can Democrats stop Trump’s tariffs?

▪ The Hill : Do the midterms change the calculus for permitting reform?

WAITING GAME : Final votes are still being tallies in the two remaining uncalled Senate races.

Even as Democrats have already clinched a comfortable majority in the Senate, the results of Mississippi and Alaska’s contests could be critical in padding their edge and determining what the 2028 Senate battle will look like.

Democrat Scott Colom ‘s lead in Mississippi’s race ticked up to close to 3,000 votes to end last week, boosting Democratic hopes that he will oust incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R). If Colom holds on, he will be the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since the 1980s.

Outstanding ballots can still be counted through the end of Tuesday as long as they were postmarked by Election Day. But with the final count likely to be razor-tight, a complicated legal situation could follow.

You can read more here from Morning Report’s Sarah Fortinsky on how Colom turned the race into a nail-biter.

Democrat Mary Peltola has maintained her narrow lead over incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in Alaska, but she’s short of a majority of the vote. As ballots can still be counted for 10 more days and Alaska uses ranked choice voting, the public might not know the winner until close to Thanksgiving.

▪ The Hill : Democrats see new path to expand Senate majority in 2028.

▪ The Hill : Alaska governor gives vote count update on Senate race.

JUST KIDDING : UFC President and CEO Dana White is meeting with Trump today to discuss his offer to become the next White House press secretary.

But Trump told reporters Sunday evening he was joking about making the cage fighting mogul his chief spokesperson.

“Of course, I was kidding. And you can see that, because they put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all gonna come with them. But it was, it was just a little fun,” Trump said.

The president has been without a press secretary since Katie Zacharia ‘s brief five-day stint in the job before she was dismissed following a widely criticized tenure.

Trump and White have been close friends for years, and they collaborated to host a UFC fight on the White House South Lawn in June as part of the country’s 250th birthday celebrations.

▪ The Hill : Trump shares cartoon of White as press secretary.

The president will meet with the Qatari prime minister at noon.

The U.S. Supreme Court is seen on Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. (Mariam Zuhaib, Associated Press)

PATH OBSTRUCTED : The incoming Democratic Senate majority will cause the president to lose the glidepath he’s enjoyed to getting his judicial nominees confirmed.

Following last week’s results, pressure quickly rose on Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito to retire, but they haven’t indicated interest in imminently doing so.

Schumer has signaled that his party could serve as a roadblock if a vacancy arises on the high court during the next two years.

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” he told The Associated Press.

The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports that this would mark a major shift in the dynamic after remaking the federal judiciary was one of Trump’s most lasting legacies from his first term.

Trump successfully nominated three justices to the Supreme Court during his first administration — Neil Gorsuch , Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett . He also helped remake the lower courts, nominating dozens of judges.

By this point in his first term, the Senate had confirmed 83 of Trump’s judicial nominees, according to data from the Federal Judicial Center. But the pace of confirmation has been slower during the second term, reaching 56 so far.

That’s led some Republicans to call for a quicker push to fill the current vacancies, Schonfeld notes.

The federal judiciary’s administrative office reports that there are 28 district court vacancies waiting to be filled, with nominees pending for 11 of them.

▪ The Hill : Prosecutor in office housing ‘grand conspiracy’ probe resigns.

▪ The Hill : Sonia Sotomayor hopes court overturns immunity decision.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog, right, tasks Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government at the president’s residence in Jerusalem on Nov. 8, 2026. (Ohad Zwigenberg, Associated Press)

FIRST UP : Israeli President Isaac Herzog has chosen opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to have the first shot at forming a government following Israel’s parliamentary elections at the end of last month.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ‘s current coalition finished first in the elections but fell short of a majority, giving an opening to Eisenkot, who appears to have a clearer path to forming a government. Herzog is tasked as the president with choosing who to give a mandate to, and it doesn’t need to be the party leader with the most seats in the Knesset.

The pressure will now be on Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, to gather enough backing from multiple parties to form a government. He has 28 days to do so, but the window can be extended by 14 more days.

Eisenkot can form a government with the parties currently in his coalition and the two major Arab party coalitions, but that’s easier said than done. He’s laid out four principles that anyone joining his government must agree to, but the Arab parties aren’t fully on board with them.

They all seem to recognize a shared goal of ousting Netanyahu, but the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu has signaled it would refuse to be in a government with the Arab parties.

One of the Arab-led parties, the Joint List, has offered to back Eisenkot from outside the government to get Netanyahu out.

▪ The Jerusalem Post : Antony Blinken says he warned Netanyahu about losing support.

▪ The Atlantic : Democrats’ fight over Israel is just beginning.

Democrats won — now they must clean house , David Wippman and Glenn C. Altschuler write in The Hill.

It was the economy, not the war , Mark Penn and Andrew Stein write in The Wall Street Journal.

James Talarico, the newly elected Democratic Texas senator, speaks at an election night event in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Eric Gay, Associated Press)

And finally … Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico (D) made a surprise appearance during “Saturday Night Live” over the weekend.

Talarico appeared during the open of the show’s first episode following the midterms, which started out featuring cast members playing Schumer and Jeffries celebrating the Democrats’ wins. They were then interrupted by James Austin Johnson playing Trump, who mentioned the president’s nickname for the incoming senator, “Talafreako.”

Talarico then interrupted by walking out from the wings and saying, “That’s Sen. Talafreako.” He introduced himself as “the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5″ and made a joke the frequent Trump bit before kicking off the show with,”Live from New York, it’s Saturday Night.”

The current state legislator is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

articles.title: Joe Biden, in White House memoir, says Trump should carry the weight of Jan. 6 riots 'to his grave'
articles.summary: President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with...
articles.body:
ATLANTA (AP) — Former U.S. President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."

And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump's years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should "follow him to his grave."

Biden's sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of "Promise Me, America," published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president's full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment , his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.

"Donald Trump led an insurrection," Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the U.S. Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. "His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.

"The rioters weren't 'peaceful protesters," he wrote. "They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election." He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons of the offenders.

"To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they're supporters of law enforcement," Biden wrote. "Here's my view: You don't get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave."

Biden also laments Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.

"All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors," Biden wrote. "In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else's accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down."

Democrats won big but Biden's reputation still lags

The memoir's release comes on the heels of Biden's fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump's second presidency. But Trump's return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden's one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party.

In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, "the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them."

During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden's vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November.

Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he'd been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he "won't be able to do as many conversations about my book as I'd hoped" and urging people to let the book speak for him.

Biden said his doctors "continue to be encouraged by how I've responded to treatment." But, he acknowledged, "Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down."

Biden tells of an unusually complimentary Trump

In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots.

"'You know, Joe, if it weren't for politics, I believe we'd be good friends,'" Trump said, according to Biden.

Trump even commented "that he'd been relieved he didn't have to run against me," Biden added.

Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win.

Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump "a tour of the world," including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-U.S. relations. Biden said Trump "focused on the personalities" of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations.

He said that two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump's opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a "crueler government" that "tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds" and a president who "took a wrecking ball to our traditions."

The title echoes Biden's memoir about his late son

The memoir's title echoes an earlier Biden book, "Promise Me, Dad," that he wrote about his son Beau's cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president's age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy.

In that first book, released between Biden's vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014.

"Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you're going to be all right," Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later.

In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the U.S. is unique because it was "built on an idea" that "all of us are created equal."

"Promise me, America," he concluded, that "we'll never forget it."

articles.title: Yemen is Iran’s new front for regional conquest
articles.summary: Yemen is not a sideshow.
articles.body:
Every American knows the word “mocha,” but few know that it is a city in Yemen.

For three centuries, Mocha was the coffee port from which the rest of the world received aromatic beans from their point of origin in Kaffa Province , Ethiopia. Tradition credits Shaykh al-Shadhili, the Sufi holy man said to have brought coffee drinking to Arabia, with its founding .

From Mocha, the beans traveled north to Turkish coffee houses. In 1683, they reached the Ottoman siege of Vienna, where legend says a spy named Georg Franz Kolschitzky opened the city’s first café with sacks the retreating Turks left behind. The first license actually went to an Armenian, Johannes Diodato .

So every chocolatey coffee in America now owes its name to a Sufi saint’s harbor on the Red Sea.

On Sept. 10, Yemen’s Houthi militiamen seized Mocha after government troops withdrew. From there, these Iranian proxy fighters pushed toward the islands of the Bab al-Mandab, the strait where the Red Sea meets the Indian Ocean. Houthi electronic warfare units, with Iranian help, impersonated government commanders over the radio and ordered the defenders to pull back.

Iran’s parliament speaker celebrated the same day. Tehran told Pakistan that “Iran does not control the Houthis,” then acknowledged that the offensive served Iran by raising oil prices and Washington’s costs.

I am a Muslim and a human rights activist, and I refuse to call any of this “Yemen’s civil war.” A proxy Tehran arms, aids, cheers, and profits from is a proxy under the Ayatollahs’ control.

One month later, the war reached Riyadh. On October 10, a missile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport, killing at least 12 people and wounding 309 . Among the dead was an American . Most were Muslims, and all were innocent. It was the fourth strike in five days on the airport, which remained closed for more than a week before a partial reopening. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the American death and condemned the attack “by the terrorist Houthis,” which he said, “took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen.”

Yemen is the front that Iran chose after Israel shut down the others, and Americans are already dying on it.

Why Yemen, and why now? Because Israel has severely diminished what were long the two most terrible arms of the Iranian octopus. For two decades, Hamas and Hezbollah held a check on America’s freedom to act in the Middle East. Then Hamas murdered 1,200 people during its Oct. 7, 2023 invasion of Southern Israel, including 49 Americans , and dragged roughly 250 hostages into Gaza, 12 of them Americans. The invaders raped and mutilated women and girls, as the United Nations has documented.

In response, Israel has now gutted Hamas. And in September 2024, it blew up Hezbollah’s pagers in its operatives’ pockets and, ten days later, killed their leader, Hassan Nasrallah .

Oct. 23 marked 43 years since Hezbollah bombed the Marine barracks in Beirut and killed 241 Americans . President Trump said it plainly on the 35th anniversary: Hezbollah carried out the attack, and Iran founded Hezbollah and still funds it. That is Iran’s four-decade-old shadow war on America.

Incomplete victories over two of Iran’s proxy terrorist groups did not end the struggle, though. They merely shifted Iran’s focus from Gaza and Lebanon to the Arabian Peninsula.

Before they struck Riyadh, the Houthis had warned the airlines. Their spokesman ordered every carrier out of Saudi airspace, “with the exception of Mecca and Medina .” So a militia in Sana’a now decides which of the Kingdom’s airports the world may use, and grants the holy cities an exemption as if it were their custodian.

Lufthansa, Air France-KLM, Qatar Airways, Etihad, Air India, and Cathay Pacific all suspended service to Riyadh. The FAA told American carriers to exercise caution over Saudi Arabia through mid-December. Delta postponed its first Atlanta-to-Riyadh flight to March.

Iran’s proxy closed Arabia’s sky, and the world’s airlines accepted its terms.

Air travel over the Peninsula is not as safe as it once was. Just weeks earlier, on September 30, the co-pilot of Flydubai Flight 1073, Dubai to Tel Aviv, had attacked his captain with a crash axe and tried to seize the controls of a jet carrying 174 passengers . Israeli officials say he applied to Flydubai after researching airlines that fly to Tel Aviv . He went looking for a cockpit pointed at Israel and found one in the Gulf. Trump said he was linked to Iran, “based on what I’m hearing .”

Just read the Houthi banner , which says, in full: “God is great. Death to America. Death to Israel. A curse upon the Jews. Victory to Islam.”

As a Muslim, I say what I believe in my soul: There is no victory for Islam in a curse. A movement that writes one in God’s name has told you what it is. Its patrons are no subtler — Iran’s parliament has chanted “Death to America” on the floor, on camera.

Look at the map. Iran has choked the Strait of Hormuz on one side of the Arabian Peninsula. Its proxy now sits at the Bab al-Mandab on the other, able to pressure two of the world’s most strategic chokepoints at once. How did it come to this? Saudi Arabia and the U.S. each waited for the other to stop the Houthis, and neither did . The bill arrived in a Riyadh departure hall on October 10.

Yemen is not a sideshow. It is the port from which Iran means to strangle the Red Sea and begin its march to regional conquest. Only America can close that front, and America must.

Bassem Eid is a Palestinian human rights activist living in the West Bank.

articles.title: Democrats must deliver, not just investigate
articles.summary: We have kicked the moneychangers out of democracy’s temples. Now, the new Congress must respond in ways that keep the new alignment alive.
articles.body:
In the post-mortem period of the midterm elections, pundits and politicians offered a variety of ideas about what caused the blue wave and what it means. My favorite is the theory that voters have launched a democracy-saving realignment in American politics and government.

We have kicked the moneychangers out of democracy’s temples. Now, the new Congress must respond in ways that keep the new alignment alive.

One impulse is to launch multiple investigations of the Trump administration’s historic corruption, demonstrating that even the richest and most powerful crooks and capitulators will be held accountable for betraying the public trust.

The danger is that the investigations will come across as the same retribution politics that Donald Trump practices, rather than addressing what middle America cares about. Congressional oversight is important and long overdue. But Democrats will keep the election’s momentum alive only by solving grassroots problems.

In the process, they should invite their Republican colleagues to start serving the people rather than Trump. Trump doesn’t worry about reelection in 2028, but congressional Republicans do. Democrats should challenge them to help override Trump’s likely vetoes, particularly if MAGA turns out to be in shambles. It’s a long shot, but worth a try.

In any case, the new Democratic majorities should start the 120th Congress with a crisp agenda that addresses the midterms’ prominent issues, like corruption, the war, affordability, health care, and the Epstein files.

Corruption: Oversight committees should identify and fix the gaps and loopholes in laws and conventions that Trump and his collaborators exploited for profit, favors and other abuses. For example, the president and vice president are exempt from the criminal conflict-of-interest law that applies to other executive branch officials. Congress should eliminate the exemption , and require presidents to place their financial assets in independently administered blind trusts and disclose the income, assets and debts of businesses in which they or their family have substantial interests

Affordability : Trump’s tariffs are a hidden tax on businesses and consumers. They cost an average of $1,000 per household in 2025 and $820 this year . Tariffs are Congress’s responsibility under the Constitution, but lawmakers have delegated too much authority to the executive branch. They should take some back.

Purse strings: Trump has defied Congress’s authority over federal spending, using a “ pocket rescission ” to block billions of dollars lawmakers appropriated for programs that serve minority groups, immigrants and housing. Lawmakers should make sure the executive branch faithfully executes their appropriations.

Energy independence: The Iran war reminds us how fragile an economy is when fossil fuels provide 82 percent of its energy consumption. The war’s interruption of global oil supplies has driven up energy prices by more than $153 billion, or $1,175 per household , since the war began.

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 included $369 billion for clean energy investments, helping homeowners and communities afford solar and wind energy and electric vehicles. Trump defied the law by withholding more than $7.5 billion , primarily from Democrat-leaning states . His 2025 budget bill canceled $82 billion more in clean energy investments, sacrificing nearly 500,000 future jobs. Congress should restore the funds.

Military operations: Congress should assert greater oversight on Trump’s use of military force. As of September, the Pentagon had conducted more than 70 strikes on boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean and killed more than 240 people in what some legal experts contend are war crimes. The administration has refused to release a legal opinion it claims justifies these killings. Congress should compel the administration to provide it.

Immigration: Congress should approve the bipartisan immigration reform bill it developed in 2024. Republicans dropped it, reportedly at Trump’s direction . Lawmakers should claw back unspent money from the $170 billion they appropriated for immigration enforcement in the 2025 budget act. They should withhold the funds until the Department of Homeland Security reforms its enforcement and deportation practices, including due process for immigrants, decent detention facilities, an independent ombudsman for detainees, and transparent investigations of alleged abuses by ICE agents.

Health care: The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy observes that every income group except the richest 1 percent is paying more because of Trump’s tax and economic policies. Congress should pull back the tax cuts in the 2025 budget bill to restore Republican cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act.

Epstein files: Congress should cite Attorney General Todd Blanche for contempt for failing to release 2.5 million pages of Epstein files he is withholding in apparent violation of the Epstein Files Transparency Act. It should pass pending legislation allowing states and survivors to sue the Justice Department for inadequate compliance with the act.

Winning power is one thing; earning public trust is another. Democrats have achieved the first goal. Now they must accomplish the other one.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Democrats won big — why and what comes next may matter more
articles.summary: The Democratic landslide was more about frustration with Trump and Republicans than a Democratic vision and agenda.
articles.body:
On Tuesday night, voters across the country sent a decisive message to President Donald Trump and Republicans: We’re fed up and want change. Large as Democrats’ victory was, the real message was that Republicans simply collapsed.

Indeed, that is the overarching takeaway from a midterm election that saw Democrats retake the House and the Senate, flipping a number of seats in deep-red states including Texas, North Carolina, Kansas and South Carolina where they have not won in decades.

Moreover, even Republican-friendly redistricting in a number of states could not save Republicans. In Florida, where Republicans intended to carve out four safe seats, Democrats won all four, and all in districts Trump won by nine or more points in 2024.

That said, the Democratic landslide was more about frustration with Trump and Republicans than a Democratic vision and agenda.

Across every age bracket, a majority or plurality of voters said their midterm vote was “to express opposition to President Trump” according to the Associated Press’s voter poll . This was most pronounced among young voters ages 18-29 years old, 60 percent of whom said their vote was a rejection of Trump, but even among voters older than 65, nearly 4 in 10 (39 percent) said the same.

Likewise, corruption emerged as a key issue. A majority of voters called government corruption “crucial” to their vote, far outpacing concerns about the war with Iran, AI, and immigration enforcement.

Two data points from the poll — which surveyed 80,000 voters in all 50 states — underscores the point that the midterms were more of a repudiation of Trump than an embrace of Democrats.

First, over 60 percent of voters believe Trump’s policies have directly damaged the economy, and “ almost two-thirds said inflation was up because of Trump’s policies.” Having been elected largely due to promises to tame inflation, tariffs and the fallout from the Iran war have done the opposite, and voters made their opposition clear.

Second, 53 percent of voters have an unfavorable view of Democrats, yet they were so angry at the administration, they voted for Democratic candidates anyway.

Both of these were evident in the large swings from 2024. Across all voters, there was a 15-point shift in favor of Democrats compared to two years ago. In fact, every single major demographic group swung towards Democrats: Hispanics by 28, Asians by 17, whites by 13 and Blacks by 9.

It also cut across demographics and geographies that have been key to Trump’s base. After shifting to Republicans by 23 points in 2024, young men swung nearly 40 points back to Democrats this year. Among men without a college degree, the swing to Democrats was 19 points, a remarkable change in just two years. And in counties that Trump won in 2024, there was an average 8-point swing to the Democrats, per the Politico poll.

Democrats should recognize that these swings can be temporary — they were on the wrong side of them in 2024. Thus, it’s critical they now turn to governing rather than waging all-out partisan warfare. Put another way, Democrats should not mistake their victory for a mandate. They won because Trump lost, not because their agenda was compelling.

To that end, Democrats’ incoming Senate majority is partly built on the back of progressives like Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, Texas State Rep. James Talarico, Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed — though some Democrats did win competitive races by winning over disaffected Republicans. Looking at the data, it’s apparent that while those three all won their races, they underperformed their more moderate fellow Democrats.

Democrats won the national popular vote by roughly 13 points , but in Michigan, Minnesota and Maine — all states with progressive Senate candidates — the Democrats markedly underperformed their moderate counterparts such as Roy Cooper in North Carolina and even Talarico in Texas.

Likewise, in Michigan, El-Sayed won nearly 100,000 less votes than Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, and in Maine, Troy Jackson did not improve on Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins in a blue wave year. That balance may prove to be one of the election’s most consequential outcomes.

Because Democrats won commanding — rather than narrow — majorities, the radical left candidates will have less power to dictate the agenda. Democratic leaders now have a genuine opportunity to govern from the pragmatic center and pursue policies that can both pass Congress and command broader public support.

That opportunity could be squandered if party leaders allow radical Democrats to conduct endless investigations of the president, his administration and his family. Instead, Democrats can provide necessary oversight without causing paralysis, while focusing on practical solutions to the economic and governing failures that drove voters away from Republicans.

Ultimately, midterms are typically referendums on the president, and the 2026 elections were no different. Voters felt betrayed, angry, and demanded change, then handed Democrats the largest popular vote victory since Watergate .

What Democrats do with their newfound power remains to be seen, but for the good of the party, and indeed the country, they should work to build solutions to the problems voters want addressed.

For their part, Republicans will have to find a way to regain voters’ trust after a historic repudiation of their party.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”

articles.title: Senate Republican calls for delayed leadership election
articles.summary: Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.), a more moderate Republican from a key battleground state, is endorsing a call by conservative Senate GOP colleagues to delay the party’s leadership elections scheduled for Tuesday. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of…
articles.body:
Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.), a more moderate Republican from a key battleground state, is endorsing a call by conservative Senate GOP colleagues to delay the party’s leadership elections scheduled for Tuesday .

“As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” McCormick wrote late Sunday in a statement. “We need leadership in place fast, but Tuesday is too soon.”

“I know it’s been the practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it,” he added.

The Pennsylvania Republican called last week’s midterm election “the worst election result” for Republicans “in decades.”

“We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” he wrote online.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) last week collected the signatures he needed for a letter he plans to send Monday to Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton (Ark.) demanding a conference meeting to discuss pausing the leadership election.

“We need to have serious discussions within our conference as to what we can do to improve the outcome in 2028,” Johnson and his colleagues wrote.

“Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice,” they continued. “It is certainly not the way leadership elections should be conducted in the world’s most deliberative body.”

Johnson wants the Republican conference to “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding any leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt.”

He also noted Republicans senators need to map out their “strategy” to “counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Senate Steering Committee Chair Mike Lee (R-Utah) has also called for postponing the Republican leadership election.

“We have no business holding Senate Republican leadership elections until: 1) we’ve had ample opportunity to discuss what happened on Tuesday, and 2) we know who’s going to be in our conference,” Lee posted on the social platform X last week.

Senate conservatives attempted to postpone GOP leadership elections after the 2022 midterm election and the 2024 presidential election but failed to convince a majority of their Republican colleagues to do so.

The Senate GOP conference is planning to meet Tuesday morning, and Johnson, McCormick and Lee will have a chance to pitch the caucus on the possibility of halting the contest.

If they don’t get enough support, the senators will cast their ballots for the new leadership team for the next Congress later in the morning.

As of now, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) doesn’t face a challenger and is expected to easily be reelected.

articles.title: Hundreds gather in Philadelphia for Pro-Palestinian demonstration and counterprotest
articles.summary: Protesters and counterprotesters clashed in Philadelphia’s Rittenhouse Square on Sunday during a demonstration involving a boycott of Jewish-owned businesses, resulting in minor injuries to two police officers and the arrest of a teenager.
articles.body:
PHILADELPHIA ( WPHL ) — Large crowds of protesters and counterprotesters gathered in Philadelphia’s Rittenhouse Square area Sunday afternoon, with both sides making their positions known amid growing tensions surrounding a controversial boycott demonstration.

According to Philadelphia police, approximately 300 pro-Palestinian demonstrators and 200 counterprotesters were in the area.

Organizers of the boycott bike ride said the demonstration was intended to show solidarity with Palestinians and protest six Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia that they contend have supported Israel.

Meanwhile, counterprotesters gathered to show their support for the businesses targeted by the boycott, drawing long lines of customers to several locations throughout the area.

Despite efforts by Philadelphia police to keep the opposing groups separated, several confrontations broke out during the demonstration.

Police reported that two officers sustained minor injuries. A 17-year-old was also arrested and charged with assaulting police.

State and local leaders acknowledged the demonstrators’ constitutional right to peaceful protest while condemning the targeting of Jewish-owned businesses.

Jewish community leaders urged people to respond with love and support for the businesses and communities affected. Meanwhile, boycott organizers said they firmly oppose racism and all forms of oppression.

“The only way to push back at hate is to show love; that’s what you’re seeing here with this huge line back here,” Michael Balaban, president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia, told Action News at 10 on PHL17.

Organizers say another boycott bike ride is expected to take place Sunday.

articles.title: Losing Congress won’t make Trump a lame duck — it will make him a wrecking ball
articles.summary: Trump has shown us what he’s willing to do and how he bends the rules when his party controls Congress. But we ain’t seen nothing yet.
articles.body:
Last week, America delivered a resounding defeat to President Trump’s MAGA agenda . Trump has since vacillated in response to the results, saying that “the Democrats did a good job ” and that he will work with them, while also threatening to use his “ tremendous powers ” to veto Democratic policies.

Trump has shown us what he’s willing to do and how he bends the rules when his party controls Congress. But we ain’t seen nothing yet.

Historical precedent and conventional political wisdom say that Trump losing control of Congress will relegate him to the ultimate ignominy of being a lame-duck president presiding over a divided government. That’s unlikely to be Trump’s fate.

Counterintuitively, losing the midterms may keep Trump popularly relevant and save him from the usual presidential fade into oblivion. While he’ll get less and less cooperation from Capitol Hill, he’ll be relatively released from the burdens of governing and free to pursue the attention that he so desperately craves. For Trump, the surest way to get that attention is to pick a fight.

Losing the midterms won’t make Trump weaker — it will only make him more aggressive.

Part of the reason is temperament: Governing is hard , and Trump has always been more at home at the rally podium than behind the Resolute Desk. That preference has been indulged more often this term: loyalists have replaced the first administration’s “adults in the room,” and Trump doesn’t have another election ahead of him — at least, not a constitutional one — to moderate him.

Government institutions and groups within those institutions like the YOLO Caucus , made up of senators freed from reelection considerations, have somewhat constrained Trump thus far. Earlier this year, for instance, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) blocked the confirmation of a new Fed chair until Trump dropped his punitive investigation of Jerome Powell .

There is always the possibility that Trump will roll over and go along with traditionally Democratic policies. But with no hope of exerting substantive control over a Democratic Congress for the remainder of his time in office, it is more likely that Trump will soon become essentially unfettered — a YOLO president, if you will.

Thus far, a friendly legislative branch has constrained him only at the margins. Even with his party in control, Trump prefers the bull-in-a-china-shop approach. And when that approach is stymied, he has waded into defying Congress outright, offering only token, narrow deference when the legal ambiguity can’t be pushed any further.

In February, Trump launched the Iran war without congressional authorization . When the 60-day War Powers Resolution deadline arrived, his administration argued that an April ceasefire had ended the clock . When the ceasefire collapsed in July, he sent a notice calling the renewed strikes a separate operation, restarting the clock .

For two straight years , the White House has canceled money that Congress appropriated by letting the funds expire before lawmakers could vote on the request. The Government Accountability Office has twice found this type of “pocket rescission” illegal .

We also have seen what happens when the legislature isn’t so friendly. Trump lost the House once before , and the two years that followed gave us the then-longest-ever government shutdown , a national emergency declaration to spend border wall money Congress refused to authorize, and two impeachments .

This Democratic Congress will end any chance of his legislative priorities passing. Holding the purse strings on every spending bill, it will also provide a useful foil to Trump and will likely supercharge his use of executive orders — or straight-up defiance of Congress. Most usefully for Trump, it will give him a seemingly reasonable justification with presidential precedent: The legislature is gridlocked, so he has to act alone, using the same “ pen and phone ” argument Barack Obama made when lawmakers stalled him.

The next two years of Democrats’ subpoenas and appropriations oversight will likely be embarrassing and painful, but as the border wall “ emergency ” showed, they’ll have limited actual effect. Impeachment will likely be on the docket at some point. But without the requisite 67 votes to convict and remove Trump from office, a third impeachment will be no more damaging than the first two — and it will give him a major grievance to trumpet at every rally.

With policy accomplishments off the table, grievance will be the only option for Trump to stay popularly relevant, exert control over his faithful, and bask in the adoration of his base as a martyr for the cause. Without a willing legislative partner acquiescing to his efforts to redefine America and the president’s role in it, Trump will be backed into a corner where the only option he sees is to fight harder than ever.

If and when that happens, Trump will be where he’s most effective and, seemingly, most comfortable. He can leave behind the need to pretend to care about governing and simply go on another tour, raging against everything Democrats do and breaking whatever vestiges are left of our national institutions and decency.

We’ve already seen what Trump does with a Congress that goes along with him. Now we’re about to find out what he does with a Congress that won’t.

Micah Ables writes about foreign policy and U.S. politics at Conscience of a Young Conservative .

articles.title: Trump says MAGA can exist without him
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said his “Make America Great Again,” or MAGA movement can exist in American politics without his involvement. Trump sat down for an interview with “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat, who asked the president about the Republican Party’s future following its devastating losses in last week’s midterm elections. “Do you think you…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said his “Make America Great Again,” or MAGA movement can exist in American politics without his involvement .

Trump sat down for an interview with “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat, who asked the president about the Republican Party’s future following its devastating losses in last week’s midterm elections.

“Do you think you can have MAGA without you as the leader?” Douthat said.

Trump replied that he thinks so, “because MAGA is basically common sense,” echoing a line Republicans stated on the campaign trail that voters had to choose between “common sense versus crazy,” as Trump and other Republicans characterized Democrats.

The CBS host noted that Trump will likely endorse someone to carry on his legacy beginning in 2028, to which Trump first said “probably” but then added “not necessarily. We have a tremendous bench.”

Douthat then asked who would be on the president’s list of potential successors other than Vice President Vance.

“Well, I think Marco’s great, but there are many others and I’d rather not mention their names,” he said, referring to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “There’s some senators that are excellent. I know them all. I like them a lot.”

“So, I may or may not get involved,” he continued. “I don’t know. Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.”

The passage of the midterms signifies the approaching halfway point of Trump’s second term, with questions swirling about his political future and the future of the MAGA movement.

But the historic losses last Tuesday have blurred the picture of the party’s presidential field about 15 months before the GOP primaries begin. Vance is the likely heir to Trump’s legacy, but it could become difficult to sell himself as a change candidate while still being part of an increasingly unpopular administration .

The GOP’s losses and subsequent hit on the administration have created a large opening for other potential Republican primary candidates, such as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas).

Rubio, who ran against Trump for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination, fares better in hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates, according to a survey taken by Emerson College and The Hill back in August.

The secretary largely kept his distance from Trump’s midterm campaign and has not commented about the election results.

Reporting from The Independent and other outlets suggested Rubio was considering leaving the Trump administration to allegedly prepare for a 2028 presidential run. However, the State Department called this reporting a “ baseless hoax .”

The outlet report cited an unnamed “Washington insider” who claimed that Rubio should distance himself from the Iran war and that it would make sense for him to “step down and leave the administration.”

articles.title: Yes, the Midterms Were About the Iran War
articles.summary: New polling shows that voters were animated by opposition to the war—and want more congressional oversight.
articles.body:
Republicans have been debating the causes of their midterm election losses last week, which gave Democrats a lead of at least a 36 seats in the House of Representatives. One faction of the Trump administration, led by Vice President J.D. Vance, argues that the decision to attack Iran was politically fatal. Another faction, led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is arguing that Republicans actually have a mandate to defeat Iran.

New data suggests that Vance is right. According to a poll conducted right before the election by YouGov on behalf of the Institute for Global Affairs, 44 percent of Americans said that they were less likely to vote for a candidate who supported the war, compared to only 13 percent who said they were more likely. And 53 percent said that Congress should have a final say over when the war ends, compared to 29 percent who chose the president. Iran may not be the only reason the Republicans did poorly, but it certainly seems to be a major one.

The poll adds to a growing body of evidence that the war was a major electoral loser. A majority of Americans opposed the war from the beginning, and an ABC News poll showed that 34 percent of voters considered the war "crucial" to their vote. While foreign policy has usually stayed out of sight and out of mind for American voters, the fighting in the Persian Gulf dramatically drove up fuel prices this year.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in an essay the morning after the midterms. Citing an unnamed pollster, he claimed that disgruntled swing voters had four demands: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

Rubio gave a thinly-veiled reply to Vance at the Conservative Political Action Conference on Saturday. "We cannot live in a world in which the most radical, terroristic regime on the planet possesses a weapon of mass destruction. And we've had president after president ignore it and allow it to linger, but this president wasn't elected to ignore it, and he wasn't elected to allow threats to linger," he said.

Others in his camp have argued that voters were punishing President Donald Trump for failing to fight Iran hard enough. Fox News hosts Mark Levin and Mark Thiessen blamed the June 2026 peace memorandum, which they both pinned on Vance, for prolonging the war. (That deal fell apart a month later.) "We should have taken care of it, ended it, armed the Iranian people, removed the regime," said Levin, who sits on the Homeland Security Advisory Council and whose stepson is a high-level State Department official.

But the polling was clear: Fifty-three percent of voters told YouGov that the U.S. government should prioritize lower prices even if its military goals in the Middle East are not met, compared to only 22 percent who preferred meeting those military goals even if prices stay high.

Part of the problem, of course, is that the Trump administration has never really been able to stick to one story about what those goals are.

"Trump and his aides still cannot agree on what they are trying to accomplish," The New York Times reported on Sunday. Vance—who publicly said during the 2024 election, "If you're going to punch the Iranians, you punch them hard"—consistently insists that the main U.S. interest is preventing Iran from building a nuclear weapon. Rubio has claimed that the goal was preventing an Iranian bomb and destroying Iran's " defense industrial base " so it cannot wage war. Levin wants the full overthrow of the Iranian government and possibly U.S. troops in Iran. Trump himself has bounced between all of these lines.

The U.S. Constitution was never designed for wars to be decided through this kind of factional palace intrigue. Article I, Section 8, gives Congress, not the president, the power to declare war. And the YouGov poll suggests that despite Congress' dismal 25 percent approval rating, Americans trust that institution more than the White House to make such decisions. The same week as the peace memorandum, Congress voted on bipartisan lines for a resolution calling on Trump to end the war .

The next Congress has a mandate to forcefully oppose the war. Rather than passing another war powers resolution, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D–Md.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D–Calif.) are threatening to simply strip away the funding for the Trump administration to continue the conflict. But as past experience shows, Congress may not have the willpower to actually fight the president over the military budget.

Of course, the same voters who gave Democrats a mandate could as easily take it away. In the YouGov poll, 76 percent of Democratic voters said they were less likely to vote for a candidate who supported the war. And in the primaries this year, establishment favorites such as Haley Stevens and Adriano Espaillat lost to insurgent candidates who made opposing the war a big part of their pitch.

"It would be a betrayal of the voters to be complicit in keeping the war going," Van Hollen told The Washington Sun .

articles.title: Ossoff is my choice as politician of the year
articles.summary: Political analyst Juan Williams named Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia as the 2026 Politician of the Year due to his impactful social media messaging and influence on the midterm elections.
articles.body:
It is time to announce the winner of this column’s coveted “Politician of the Year” award for 2026.

Yes, I know it’s early to announce an “end of the year” award. But this is a blowout.

No other national politician had such a good year.

He gets the crown now because he had an impact beyond winning his Senate race. His imprint on the 2026 midterms went beyond Georgia, went beyond the South and changed the look of the 2028 race for president.

In this social media age, his mastery of effective political messages set a new standard.

Look at how he turned attention to corruption and the economy, the top issues for voters, and the winning issues for Democrats, in the closing weeks of the midterms campaign.

“We were told that MAGA was for working-class Americans. But this is a government of, by, and for the ultra-rich,” Ossoff said in his algorithm-friendly delivery . “This is the Epstein class, ruling our country. They are the elites they pretend to hate.”

The phrase “the Epstein Class,” became the perfect shorthand to define President Trump and his congressional allies in the age of social media.

Ossoff set off another social media frenzy when he found an eye-catching way to zing Trump for tariffs and a war that produced high prices.

Trump has no time to deal with the economy, he said , because Trump “wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”

Immediately, Trump’s mishandling of the economy had a sexy angle that went way beyond the price of gas.

The president’s young, blonde aide, Natalie Harp, was featured in news reports on her constant presence around the president. Then came reports on her lack of credentials and her letter to the president telling him, “ You are all that matters to me .”

The national press coverage and social media focus on his remarks proved to be “damaging and distracting to the [Trump] White House,” David Graham recently wrote in the Atlantic . Graham credited Ossoff, a former documentary maker, as a master of pairing “good visuals with a knack for the sound bite.”

It also inspired imitators among Democrats desperate for streetfighters to counter Trump’s use of social media.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) campaigned on a slogan of “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.”

Ossoff also demonstrated masterful messaging skill in confronting Trump’s supporters for their use of racially divisive tactics.

He created a viral media moment when he lambasted his opponent in the Senate race, GOP Rep. Mike Collins, for his ties to white supremacists .

He quipped that Collins had hired “half the Third Reich,” to work on his staff. Then he added that if the late Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.) was marching for voting rights today “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.”

That fearless attitude thrilled Democrats, especially Latino and Black Democrats. They long to see the party counter Trump’s constant attacks on immigrants. They wanted a cure for Trump’s use of divisive racial policies to stir up a far-right base.

Ossoff’s willingness to punch back at bigotry could be a preview of upcoming viral moments in the presidential race.

Vice President JD Vance, a likely 2028 candidate for the GOP nomination, has defended Republican operatives and activists who used white supremacist rhetoric in text groups.

Vance also supported Supreme Court rulings to weaken protections for minority voting rights. He even backed the lie that Haitian immigrants in Ohio were eating their white neighbors’ pets.

Ossoff is positioned as a young, 39-year-old, Jewish politician who is not afraid of his identity and willing to fight back against racist tactics. On this issue, he is in step with the sizable presence of Blacks and Latinos in the Democrats’ multiracial base of supporters.

If he runs for the Democrats’ presidential nomination, Ossoff has allies among Black politicians. He is close to fellow Georgians, Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock, and the incoming governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms.

They could help deliver Black support in early primaries to Ossoff in much the same way Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) did for Vice President Biden in the 2020 primaries .

It was that same mobilization of conservative Black voters in the South that led to Biden’s win over Trump and earned Clyburn my award for best politician of 2020 .

Similarly, look for Ossoff to win attention as a star of upcoming congressional hearings aimed at holding Trump administration officials accountable for pressuring big corporations for donations.

On the Senate Intelligence panel, he will be at the center of Democrats’ efforts to finally force Trump special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to explain how their business deals in the Middle East are tied to U.S. national security.

His seat on the Senate Appropriations Committee will allow him to question contracts the Trump administration gave to companies owned or controlled by the Republican Party’s largest donor, Elon Musk.

There are also the defense contractors with suspiciously cozy relationships to the president’s sons.

Sen. Ossoff is the Politician of the Year for 2026.

He may well be the Democrats’ man for a 2028 run to win the White House.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10 1/2 years for rape and sexual assaults
articles.summary: Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 1/2 years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
articles.body:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 1/2 years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during a period when his comedy career built around boasts of erotic exploits was taking off.

Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand that he showed a “casual and arrogant disregard” for any woman who said no to him.

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Bennathan said. “You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

Brand showed little emotion during the hearing and turned to mouth the words “we’ll be OK” to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers.

The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and behavior on television and radio broadcasts, along with drug and alcohol battles, had maintained his innocence and said all his encounters were consensual.

But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame.

“He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity,” Karmy-Jones said.

Brand supported by wife, father and fans outside court

Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand.

Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand’s good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse.

Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, who entered the courthouse without him, and his father, Ron Brand. Russell Brand had been free during the trial but was jailed following Thursday’s verdict.

A couple of Brand’s supporters who reflected his recent conversion to Christianity held a banner bearing crosses with the words: “Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.”

Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public

The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.

One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the impact of the crime and the others provided statements read by the prosecutor.

A woman Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like “damaged goods.”

“For many years as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke,” she said. “There were many times I felt visibly sick at the sight of him parading around thinking he can get away with anything.”

Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke out of view, hidden from the public behind a curtain to preserve her identity.

A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking.

She said it took years for her to speak up and that she only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary.

“I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed,” she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. “His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless.”

Winter, the defense lawyer, tried to minimize the significance of the rape, saying Brand should be “regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given” following consensual sex.

A woman he was convicted of kissing and groping at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 said it had a lasting impact on her life.

“Since the sexual assault … Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget,” she said. “Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump.”

The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who said the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.

“Immediately after the incident I spoke up, and sadly it was brushed under the carpet by senior management,” she said. “There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore, which meant I did not give myself time to lament on it, boxed it up and pushed it aside.”

Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men’s bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.

The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

In recent years, he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

articles.title: Alabama ended judicial override. Will it spare the prisoners left behind?
articles.summary: No one else should go to their death in Alabama because a single person thought they knew better than a group of 12 jurors.
articles.body:
On Oct. 20, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey did something quite unusual for the chief executive of a deep-red and pro-death-penalty state: She commuted the death sentence of Toforest Johnson, who had been convicted of the 1995 murder of Deputy Sheriff William Hardy.

This was the third time Ivey had used her clemency power to spare the life of someone awaiting execution. As she explained to the media, “’When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death. My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.’”

But there is another circumstance to which Ivey should now attend as she seeks to ensure justice “could effectively be delivered through capital punishment” — namely the fact that two dozen people are on her state’s death row because the judges in their trials ignored juries’ recommendations that their lives be spared.

That process is called “judicial override.” At one time or another, it was authorized for use in capital cases in only four states: Alabama, Delaware, Florida and Indiana. But attorney Meghann Lamb explains that Alabama’s judicial override statute was unique because “it did not provide judges with clear standards to determine when judicial override was appropriate.”

Today, Alabama is the only one of those states carrying out executions that resulted from judges overriding jury verdicts.

While it was originally thought of as a device to protect defendants in capital cases from jury verdicts driven by anger and emotion, it became something entirely different. It allowed judges, who are elected in Alabama, to show their own tough-on-crime credentials by sentencing convicts to death, even where juries voted for life sentences instead.

Black defendants were also more likely to be on the losing end of judicial overrides than were white defendants. Lamb reports that “Studies have shown that only six percent of ‘murders in Alabama involve Black defendants and white victims,’ but thirty-one percent of the state’s judicial override cases involve a ‘defendant of color’ and a white victim.”

Alabama’s unjust and racially discriminatory judicial override system ended in April 2017, when, on her first day in office, Ivey signed legislation abolishing judicial override. She did so even though the Alabama Supreme Court had upheld judicial override the previous October.

Alabama was the last state to abolish it. But the repeal of judicial override was not made retroactive. Since its repeal, Alabama has continued to carry out executions that resulted from judges overriding jury verdicts. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall defends that practice, arguing that “The fact that Alabama made future juries’ judgments binding does not show a societal will to undo long final sentences, for the democratically elected legislature specifically chose not to retroactively apply the new sentencing regime to prisoners already on death row.”

In 2024, state Rep. Chris England (D) introduced a bill in the Alabama House of Representatives to apply the repeal of judicial override retroactively. He reportedly told his colleagues , “We all decided that judicial override was wrong, and we repealed that section. The only right thing to do, in my opinion, is to afford everybody who was sentenced by judicial override the opportunity to be resentenced.”

But the Judiciary Committee of the Alabama House of Representatives was not persuaded, and rejected England’s proposal.

The AP quotes one of the opponents of the retroactivity legislation as saying, with no hint of irony: “’The law that was in effect at the time allowed judicial override. These judges, in their discretion, overrode. Consequently, it’s very difficult for me to second guess or in effect override that.’”

And no court has ever reduced the sentence of someone whose death sentence was imposed through override.

So, the ball is in Ivey’s court. Ivey isn’t running again, and her term ends in January.

Freed from political constraints, governors have often used their last months in office to exercise their clemency power in capital cases. Alabama’s governor should do likewise.

Ivey has already shown herself willing to use that power to rectify miscarriages of justice. She should see and rectify the injustice of carrying out the death sentences of the two dozen people sentenced under a now repealed statute.

No one else should go to their death in Alabama because a single person thought they knew better than a group of 12 jurors.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.
