articles.title: Voters’ rebuke of Trump gives Democrats historic opportunity and responsibility
articles.summary: What an unforgettable election night! The American people delivered an enthusiastic, undeniable rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party that remade itself in his image. Democrats now have a responsibility to make the most of the opportunity voters have given them. Trump’s second term has been characterized by the president’s arrogance, recklessness,…
articles.body:
The American people delivered an enthusiastic, undeniable rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party that remade itself in his image. Democrats now have a responsibility to make the most of the opportunity voters have given them.

Trump’s second term has been characterized by the president’s arrogance, recklessness, self-enrichment, abuse of power, broken promises and indifference to the harm his policies have been imposing on American families, farmers, workers and communities. And by Republicans cheering him on.

Trump and his allies promised they would uphold the rule of law by deporting violent criminals — the worst of the worst. Instead, Trump and the Republican Congress unleashed a brutal, lawless, campaign of violence against teachers, preachers, pastors, shopkeepers and parents. They inflicted a show-me-your-papers regime on brown people and communities, and used deadly violence to punish anyone, regardless of citizenship, who resisted them.

Trump promised to prioritize relief for families struggling to keep up with the high cost of living. Instead, he and congressional Republicans passed a budget that prioritized giveaways to the richest people in history — paid for by cutting millions of families’ access to food and affordable healthcare. When Trump’s trade wars and real wars — more broken promises — made things even worse, he essentially told Americans they should be grateful to be living in his delusional “ golden age .”

And when polls started to make it clear that voters weren’t buying it, Republicans tried to resort to Trump’s old playbook one more time — hoping to win voters back with smears and fearmongering about communism, Sharia law and transgender people.

It didn’t work. In fact, it failed spectacularly.

Americans rejected the corruption and cruelty. We resisted the torrent of bigotry that tried to make us fear our Muslim and transgender communities. We rejected the voices who tried to define America along exclusionary racial and religious lines.

Together, we elected a fantastically diverse group of senators, representatives, governors and state legislators who shared a vision of an America that works for all of us. So many young leaders. So many people breaking barriers for the first time.

The first Black woman ever elected governor. The first Native American woman governor and senator. The first Muslim senator. The first openly gay man in the Senate. A Latina governor in Texas. This is the multicultural democracy they irrationally fear.

And millions of Christians in traditional Republican strongholds rejected MAGA pastors and self-proclaimed prophets who tried to insist that only their version of the faith is legitimate. Right-wing Christian nationalists will have to contend with powerful progressive people of faith who voters have entrusted with power.

All these victories were grounded in organizing. The kind of long-term community organizing to which the late great Dolores Huerta devoted her life . The kind of strategic movement-building organizing led by the brilliant Stacey Abrams and the people she has mentored. The kind of solidarity-based organizing modeled by Minnesota activists who defended their neighbors from official brutality.

That kind of organizing does not and must not end on election night. It must continue to build momentum for a government that makes our lives better, not worse. For a government that serves the interests of everyday people, not just the wealthy and powerful. For a government that holds those who have abused their power and abused us accountable.

The new Democratic majorities in Congress must make clear that accountability and progress go hand in hand. They must affirm the rule of law by exposing corruption and holding lawbreakers accountable. They must take action to relieve the harms that have been imposed on the American people. And they must safeguard our future by passing needed anti-corruption, pro-democracy measures, including structural reforms for a Supreme Court that has lost Americans’ trust.

There is much work ahead. Let’s celebrate how we made that work possible and take inspiration to keep working. A lot of courageous Americans took on the world’s richest man and the world’s most powerful man — and won.

Together we have the power to build the future we dream of.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.body:
Progressives are gearing up for the 2028 election cycle with the launch of a new group meant to draw Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) into the presidential race.

Ready for AOC launched Monday aiming to demonstrate support for the popular legislator as speculation about a White House run mounts. Supporters are asked to sign a pledge to vote for Ocasio-Cortez for president, to volunteer for her campaign and to spread the word about why they want the New York Democrat to run.

“The lesser of two evils won’t deliver the landslide victory we need to pull our country back from the brink, but AOC can,” the group wrote on their website .

The democratic socialist has publicly mulled a presidential bid, as the far-left flank has notched a number of high-profile election wins across the country. She told The New York Times in September that she would make a decision after the midterm elections, adding that “sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

The 2028 Democratic primary field is bound to be crowded. Ocasio-Cortez isn’t the only progressive weighing a run either — Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) has expressed interest, and a group was recently set up to draft him into the race as well.

Ready for AOC told The Times their goal is to build a grassroots infrastructure for the congresswomen in the event she decides to run. While they do not appear to be registered with the Federal Election Commission, the group is raising money through their website.

“We believe AOC can build the coalition this moment needs, ignite the spirit of a grassroots movement, and deliver on the promises others have failed to realize,” their site reads. “We believe that together, the many can defeat the monied interests, and that a better world is possible.”

Ready for AOC will host three “welcome call” meetings over the next few weeks as they aim to grow support for their cause. Ocasio-Cortez is a close ally of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt), and she is seen as the likely successor to his progressive, populist movement.

“We know the status quo isn’t working, and that America is hungry for a different kind of candidate. A candidate who will represent the needs of the working class instead of big tech billionaires,” the group’s website reads. “A candidate who won’t fold under pressure. A candidate who is ready to deliver for the many, not the few.”

But the Oval Office isn’t the only jump the 37-year-old Ocasio-Cortez could make in 2028. She could challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for his seat or stay put in the House.

A separate political action committee, Draft AOC 2028, was established in July.

articles.title: Protecting America’s digital infrastructure starts with common sense
articles.summary: Rep. Rich McCormick has introduced the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act to direct NIST in developing updated guidance for managing cyber risks and containing breaches within modern cloud environments.
articles.body:
America has embraced cloud computing at a remarkable pace with nearly every aspect of life now running through the cloud. Businesses, hospitals, banks, and government agencies rely on cloud services to store data, run operations, and deliver critical services. As our reliance grows, so does our exposure to cyber threats. The very innovation that has transformed our economy has also created new vulnerabilities that demand our attention.

That’s why I introduced the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act . This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for securing cloud environments and assessing cyber risk in ways that reflect how modern systems actually operate.

The key challenge is not simply keeping attackers out. It’s limiting what they can do when they get in.

Think of a cloud network like a building. Strong locks, passwords, and identity checks keep intruders out. But security also depends on what happens inside. An intruder should not be able to walk into every room, access every file, or reach every critical system. The same principle applies in the cloud.

For far too long, cybersecurity has focused on preventing a breach without giving enough attention to containing one. In today’s increasingly interconnected environments, one compromised account or application should not put an entire network at risk.

Resilience matters just as much as prevention.

As a Marine Corps veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, I know firsthand that military and national security depend on the strength of the systems behind them. My work on the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee and the House AI Task Force have reinforced a critical lesson: American innovation and digital security must advance together. As technology evolves, so must our ability to protect it.

Security experts often use the term “blast radius” to describe how far an attack can spread and how much damage it can cause. A single compromised account, application or service should not become a gateway to an entire organization. Effective cybersecurity is not just about detecting threats. It is about containing them. Measuring and reducing that risk provides a more meaningful assessment of security than simply determining whether suspicious activity can be detected.

The rise of artificial intelligence — renamed “super intelligence” by President Trump’s executive order — makes this challenge even more urgent. Modern computer systems increasingly interact with multiple applications, databases and services across an organization. While these capabilities can create tremendous productivity and efficiency gains, they can also expand the potential consequences of a compromise. The more authority a system has, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on what it can access.

This is not about slowing innovation with another unnecessary layer of bureaucracy. It is about developing practical, risk-based security standards that reflect how modern cloud systems actually work and giving organizations meaningful ways to demonstrate that they are in compliance.

If effective cybersecurity means limiting the damage caused by a breach, then our standards must reflect that reality. That is why my Common-Sense Cloud Security Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for modern cloud environments, including identity management, oversight of third-party connections, detection of suspicious activity, and ways to assess the potential impact of a compromise. The bill would also establish a voluntary certification program and help ensure federal cloud security requirements keep pace with evolving technology and threats.

No law or standard can eliminate every cyber threat. What we can do is make attacks harder, limit their impact, and improve our ability to recover when they occur.

I will continue working with cybersecurity experts and industry leaders to strengthen the security of the cloud infrastructure Americans rely on every day. In today’s interconnected world, security is not measured by whether a breach occurs. It is measured by how well we contain it. Cyber threats will continue to evolve, but a single breach should never be allowed to become a systemic failure. That is the standard we should strive for as we secure America’s digital future.

Dr. Rich McCormick is a decorated veteran and Emergency Room physician who represents Georgia’s 7th District in the United States House of Representatives and serves on the House Armed Services Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee. He also serves on the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, where he is chairman of the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight.

articles.title: House Freedom Caucus urges rapid action on new reconciliation package
articles.summary: The conservative House Freedom Caucus sent a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday urging them to push through a third reconciliation package and other GOP legislative priorities before Democrats assume control of Congress next year. The caucus wrote in their letter that there is “an enormous…
articles.body:
The conservative House Freedom Caucus sent a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday urging them to push through a third reconciliation package and other GOP legislative priorities before Democrats assume control of Congress next year.

The caucus wrote in their letter that there is “an enormous amount of unfinished business to preserve and protect the Republic from an incoming majority party hell-bent on radically changing it.”

“We must deny them every legislative leverage point possible,” the caucus wrote.

The caucus is calling for a reconciliation package that includes defense modernization, tax relief for families and at least $1 trillion in spending cuts. Other priorities outlined in the letter include codifying President Trump’s border security policies, imposing congressional term limits, banning stock trading by lawmakers and confirming “as many Presidential nominees as possible” in the Senate.

Lawmakers are in session for only five more weeks until the new Congress takes over in January. The next few weeks are already consumed by leadership elections across both chambers.

Passing another reconciliation bill will also be a heavy lift. The House had passed a budget resolution for a third bill back in July that includes $73 billion for defense and intelligence funding, $12 billion for agriculture aid and $10 billion for a fund to encourage Trump-backed voting restrictions. But the resolution had been stalled in the Senate after fiscal hawk conservatives aired concerns about the lack of offsets in the package.

“Some of us called for action after our first reconciliation package to continue to move to support the American people. Unfortunately, that agenda stalled, and now we will no longer have the majority in the next Congress. We respectfully request that we take action in the next 60 days to protect the citizens we represent,” the caucus wrote, adding that lawmakers should not leave town until the objectives outlined in the letter are accomplished.

“Every one of us – including those leaving Congress on January 3rd – should be committed to finishing the job,” they added.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) lost its fourth official in the week following the midterms , with Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division Brett Shumate resigning Monday.

The Civil Division handles a wide variety of cases and has seen significant departures during the Trump administration as caseloads soared .

“Under his leadership, the Division pursued important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies and delivered key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement,” Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote on the social platform X .

“The Division also secured historic settlements to end illegal corporate DEI practices and shuttered dozens of clinics which were providing so-called ‘gender affirming care’ to minors,” Blanche continued. “We are grateful for Brett’s service at DOJ and wish him continued success.”

Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division, was the first to depart after the election.

U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, whose South Florida district oversaw the sweeping probe of the investigations into President Trump, and John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, both resigned Friday .

Shumate has overseen a number of controversial cases. These include suing universities that offered in-state tuition for undocumented citizens, defending Trump’s executive order on mail-in voting restrictions , fighting state-level laws that sought to ban federal agents from wearing masks and suing states to force them to issue undercover license plates to immigration officers.

Under the outgoing official, the Civil Division was bleeding staff, including among high-profile divisions like Appellate Staff and the Federal Programs Branch, two areas involved with defending the president’s priorities in court.

The administration has been aggressive in appealing court losses, spiking cases that must be handled by the remaining appellate staff.

The Office of Immigration Litigation also saw significant departures and a spike in cases as staff had to face habeas petitions filed by migrants demanding to be released from immigration detention.

The Commercial Litigation Branch, which handles a variety of cases, including suits from fired federal workers, saw its caseload jump 84 percent — the most of any branch.

articles.title: First challenger enters race for Fetterman’s seat in 2028

articles.body:
Less than a week after Democrats retook the Senate majority, a challenger has thrown his hat in the ring to oust one of the party’s most controversial members.

Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer and businessperson, announced a bid to unseat Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) on Monday, marking the first challenge to Fetterman as questions swirl around his allegiance to the Democratic Party.

A Gaza-born Philadelphia resident and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Moor put forth a progressive agenda as he kicked off his campaign for Senate.

“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor wrote on the social platform X. “I’m calling for accountability for genocide, for ICE and for corruption. And finally, for the protection of our civil liberties in America.”

Moor is running to the left of Fetterman, who has been more moderate since taking office, often publicly breaking with his party and drawing the ire of some Democrats. While he has said he won’t become a Republican , the Senator has warned he may leave the party if Democrats officially become anti-Israel. A poll in August showed he was more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats.

With degrees from the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard University, Moor moved to Pennsylvania with his family as a child. He worked in finance before pivoting to journalism, covering Beirut during the 2011 revolution in Egypt, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported. Moor lived in Jordan until he and his wife decided to move back to Philadelphia to raise their daughters five years ago.

“A few years ago my birthplace was turned to rubble in a genocide funded by our tax dollars, with the support of politicians on both sides of the aisle who can’t find money for transit or removing asbestos from our schools,” Moor wrote on his website .

“It’s clear the United States funds wars based on corruption and lies and has turned its back on its own people. We must make sure this never happens again. That’s why I’m running for U.S. Senate,” he added.

Fetterman has not said whether he will seek reelection in 2028. His support for sending military aid to Israel, sometimes voting with the GOP and his video appearance at the Republican midterm convention have drawn criticism among Democrats. Moor told the Philadelphia Inquirer he isn’t running against Fetterman, but rather for good governance.

“The truth is, I’m not really running against Fetterman,” Moor told the newspaper. “I’m running for good government. I’m running for the rule of law. I’m running because I believe in America. And I believe in our capacity for renewal. I believe in our capacity for redressing wrongs in our midst.”

articles.title: Kathy Hochul entertains massive political promotion as Democrats look ahead to 2028
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul says she's open to a 2028 vice presidential run, telling The New York Times she "didn't get to where I am by slamming doors."
articles.body: Fresh off her re-election victory, Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is not ruling out a spot on the 2028 Democratic presidential ticket as the party begins looking toward the next White House race. When asked by The New York Times what her response would be if a 2028 Democratic presidential hopeful was seeking a running mate, Hochul indicated she would be open to the idea. "I will say this," Hochul said. "I didn’t get to where I am by slamming doors." Hochul's comments come as Democrats begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election, with several high-profile figures floated as potential contenders, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. TOP DEMOCRAT GOVERNORS ARE HOPING TO RIDE THEIR RECORDS TO THE WHITE HOUSE. CAN THEY? articles.title: Midterm losses could accelerate Trump’s disturbing foreign policy goals
articles.summary: The big unknown is whether he will respond to the defeat in the midterm elections by “wagging the dog” and deflecting attention away from his domestic policies.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are widely viewed as a stunning rebuke of President Trump’s policies, as voters focused on the cost of living, the war with Iran and corruption. Trump’s overall stance on foreign policy, however, did not rank high on the list of voter concerns, even though his second term has been the most consequential of any administration for undermining the post-World War II order .

The unraveling began with Trump’s “ liberation day ” announcement in April 2025 that effectively terminated the international trading system that was based on the principle of most favored nation and multilateral agreements. It was replaced with a series of bilateral deals that resulted in the highest tariffs since the 1930s , which were highly unpopular with the electorate.

This was followed by the U.S. National Security Strategy report in November 2025 that called for the U.S. to strengthen the Monroe Doctrine in the Western hemisphere and to have Japan and South Korea play a greater role in defending the Western Pacific. The goal for Europe was for it to take primary responsibility for its defense, while “ending the perception, and preventing the reality, of NATO as a perpetually expanding alliance.”

Since then, Trump has taken steps to undermine the Western alliance. The latest are overt actions to support Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the war with Ukraine by calling for Volodymyr Zelensky to step down as Ukraine’s leader while exempting Russia from new sanctions and buying Russian diesel. Trump is also willing to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to settle the war with Ukraine at a meeting in China this month.

The Wall Street Journal Editorial Board views Trump’s motive as part of a larger attempt to produce a false peace . It fears that a new triumvirate that divides the world into spheres of influence would blow up America’s credibility as a reliable ally.

Meanwhile, U.S. allies are scrambling about how to align themselves. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed this issue at the Davos summit in January, when he called on middle powers to pursue strategic autonomy.

Attaining this, however, will be challenging for the European Union. When U.S. contributions to Ukraine dropped sharply in 2025, the Kiel Institute reports that European military assistance rose by 67 percent while humanitarian support increased by 59 percent from 2022-2024 averages. But political strains in Europe are increasing as the public demands more support for domestic programs.

Amid criticism that the Trump administration was undermining Ukraine, special envoy Steve Witkoff announced that the U.S. had arranged trilateral peace talks with Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week. U.S. negotiators also held talks in Brussels last week to address security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s post-war security and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction.

It is unlikely, however, that these talks will prove fruitful. Gideon Rachman of the Financial Times points out that both Witkoff and Jared Kushner are focused on getting Ukraine to cede further territory to Russia while securing U.S. business deals with Russia.

Meanwhile, financial markets have shrugged off these developments. My take is that it reflects the difficulty investors face in assessing geopolitical developments. The customary way is to formulate possible scenarios that could unfold and to assign probabilities for each of them to calculate expected returns. This approach, for example, can be used to assess the outcome of oil shocks such as the current one associated with the U.S.-Iran conflict.

However, it is much more difficult to assess the fallout from a regime shift in which the rules-based international system that prevailed for 80 years is suddenly being supplanted by a void. One cannot assign probabilities to the possible outcomes, because there is no prior experience to calculate them.

What is clear, nonetheless, is that there is heightened uncertainty today that investors must consider.

One concern is that Trump’s actions are destroying the trust many countries have placed in America’s willingness to defend themselves. Fareed Zakaria believes there is a risk that more countries will opt to develop nuclear capability to defend themselves.

There is no precedent for what is happening today, but the fragmentation within liberal democracies resembles the political unrest during the 1930s. In his book about the Great Depression, economist Charles Kindleberger argued that its breadth and depth occurred because the international economic system lacked a leader to stabilize the system. While the U.S. emerged as the world’s strongest nation, it turned inward with protectionist policies and ignored the interests of other countries.

The main risk today is that Trump appears willing to abandon America’s allies while sharing power with two of its traditional adversaries. The big unknown is whether he will respond to the defeat in the midterm elections by “ wagging the dog ” and deflecting attention away from his domestic policies.

Nicholas Sargen, Ph.D., is an economic consultant and is affiliated with the Darden Business School. He has authored three books including the 2nd edition of “ Global Shocks” .

articles.title: Fired columnist won’t return to Washington Post despite arbitration win
articles.summary: Karen Attiah will not return to her job as a Washington Post opinion columnist even after an arbitrator ruled she was unjustly fired for statements following the killing of Charlie Kirk. Attiah, who worked at the Post for 11 years as an editor and opinion writer, announced Monday she would not return due to a…
articles.body:
Karen Attiah will not return to her job as a Washington Post opinion columnist even after an arbitrator ruled she was unjustly fired for statements following the killing of Charlie Kirk.

Attiah, who worked at the Post for 11 years as an editor and opinion writer, announced Monday she would not return due to a lack of “guaranteed freedom and institutional support” within the Post newsroom. Attiah sued for wrongful termination after she was fired for writing that America “accepts and worships gun violence” and posted a quote from Kirk in which he said a number of prominent Black women didn’t have the “brain processing power” to be taken seriously.

“I have decided not to return to what The Washington Post has become. I have accepted a settlement with the Post and will move forward with my life and career,” Attiah wrote in a post to Substack on Monday. “As excruciating as this battle has been, it was one worth fighting.”

The arbitrator ruled in August that the Post did not have “good and sufficient” cause for Attiah’s termination and that they violated the organization’s collective bargaining agreement with the Post’s union. Jeff Bezos, Amazon founder and owner of the Post, said he was shifting the opinion section to cover “free markets and personal liberties.”

“My arbitration win was a monumental victory for unions, for journalists, and for free speech. As the last full-time Black columnist in the Opinions section, I recognized how important the win was for Black journalists, especially those pushed out of newsrooms in recent years,” Attiah wrote.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who supported me throughout this fight and helped me celebrate the victory. I am also indebted to the readers who have continued to believe in my work and who still believe in the power of journalism,” she added.

articles.title: Secret Service arrests two after car crash and barricade breach outside White House
articles.summary: Police arrested two individuals in separate incidents near the White House on Monday morning. The Secret Service has launched investigations into both.
articles.body: Police arrested two people outside the White House in separate incidents on Monday near Lafayette Square Park. Video from the park circulating on social media shows a vehicle that appeared to run into a barrier, with the engine emitting smoke. Authorities say the driver was "combative" with law enforcement and was arrested. "Just before 10:00 a.m., Secret Service Police and National Guard responded to the north side of Lafayette Park at 16th Street and H Street, NW, where a vehicle crashed onto the sidewalk. The driver was combative with law enforcement, but was quickly placed under arrest," a Secret Service spokesperson said in a statement. "MPD’s Explosive Ordinance Disposal team has been called to sweep the vehicle as a precaution. Subsequently, roads around Lafayette Park have been closed," the statement continued. CAR RAMS INTO WHITE HOUSE BARRICADE, SUSPECT ARRESTED: OFFICIALS "Around the same time, a second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. That individual was also quickly placed under arrest," it added. The Secret Service briefly moved reporters and the press inside the White House briefing room after the incident, but they have since been released. Authorities say both incidents are currently under investigation. The arrests come just days after authorities arrested an illegal immigrant from Venezuela outside the White House on Thursday. The Department of Homeland Security says officers found the man inside a stolen vehicle carrying multiple guns and threatening to kill President Donald Trump. U.S. Secret Service officers approached the suspect Thursday evening after spotting him "acting suspicious in his car while it was parked on Constitution Avenue in Washington, D.C.," DHS told Fox News. The suspect told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to travel to the nation's capital and kill Trump, DHS said. Officers subsequently learned that the vehicle had been reported stolen, and the suspect admitted to having weapons inside, according to DHS. A search of the vehicle reportedly turned up three guns, including an AR-15-style rifle and two handguns, along with dozens of rounds of ammunition. SECRET SERVICE DETAINS, QUESTIONS INDIVIDUAL WHO DROVE VEHICLE INTO BARRICADE NEAR WHITE HOUSE The suspect was identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who illegally entered the country through Texas in March 2024 and was subsequently arrested by U.S. Border Patrol, according to officials. He was later released into the country under the Biden administration, authorities said. After his arrest, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer for Chrinos with the U.S. Marshals Service, which currently has custody of Chrinos. articles.title: Trump calls Strait of Hormuz blockade ‘history’s greatest’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday called the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz “history’s greatest” as he mulls further strikes after the midterms. “Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, referring to the recently formed 20-member staff formed by U.S.…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday called the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz “history’s greatest” as he mulls further strikes after the midterms.

“Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , referring to the recently formed 20-member staff formed by U.S. Central Command (Centcom) Adm. Brad Cooper and tasked with “preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.”

Trump said that coupled “with history’s greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!”

The Iran war has remained at a standstill for months and has been largely unpopular among the American public. Trump and other administration officials, including Vice President Vance, have acknowledged that the conflict likely contributed to sweeping Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections last Tuesday.

On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi gave the U.S. an ultimatum after Tehran submitted a 2-day proposal to end the conflict or “choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

The U.S. reportedly launched new defensive strikes against Iran over the weekend that targeted the country’s air defense systems.

Mediators, led by Qatar, have called on Washington and Tehran to reach an agreement to end the conflict. But Trump has left open the possibility of resuming strikes, though he said Sunday that it was “ highly unlikely ” he would do so if upcoming peace talks show progress.

“I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” Trump told CNN’s Jim Sciutto. “I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them. So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to. They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.”

The weekend strikes followed up on alleged attacks on Nov. 2 that struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, home to an Iranian naval base and located in the critical Strait of Hormuz. The strikes ahead of the midterms were not publicly acknowledged by the Pentagon, which had not disclosed any attacks on Iranian targets since early September.

Trump previously determined that he would not launch strikes on Iran until after the midterms.

The president said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vance’s remarks on social media saying that Republicans lost because of the Iran war.

“He should have made one other statement,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. “One statement that I think is very important. If you had it to do again? Would you do it again? The answer is yes. I can tell you, if I had it to do again, this historically, for history, will go down as one of the best things we ever did.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, like Vance, is a potential 2028 Republican presidential primary contender, also acknowledged that the war was not “necessarily popular but necessary.”

articles.title: Senate GOP rebels move to delay leadership vote, demand reckoning after midterm disaster
articles.summary: Senate Republicans face a push from Ron Johnson and four allies to delay Tuesday's leadership elections after last week's stunning Election Night losses.
articles.body: Last week’s pummeling on Election Night has a cohort of Senate Republicans wanting to take stock as lawmakers return to Washington, D.C. The Senate GOP is slated to hold its leadership elections Tuesday morning, where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is expected to seek another term as top Republican. But a small group led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., wants to delay the leadership elections to debrief after last week’s stunning losses and chart a path forward heading into the minority. Senate Democrats flipped the chamber by clinching 54 seats, and that number could grow depending on the outcomes in Mississippi and Alaska. THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL Johnson, in a letter obtained by Fox News Digital to Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., the conference chair for the Senate GOP, argued the election should be delayed "until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats." "Tuesday's result was a stunning defeat, and there are multiple reasons for it," Johnson wrote. "We need to have serious discussions within our conference as to what we can do to improve the outcome in 2028." "Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice," he continued. "It is certainly not the way leadership elections should be conducted in the world's greatest deliberative body." GOP EYES SENATE COMEBACK AFTER DEMOCRATIC BLOODBATH, BUT ANOTHER POLITICAL NIGHTMARE COULD AWAIT The Senate GOP’s rules do allow for the consideration of such a delay, as long as Johnson can get five signatures on his letter, and he did, securing Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., John Kennedy, R-La., Ted Budd, R-N.C., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, as his base of support. "We first need to digest what happened last week and make plans to move forward," Lee said on X. "Turning to leadership elections Tuesday morning would put the cart before the horse." Others who didn’t sign onto the letter, like Sens. David McCormick, R-Pa., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., similarly want to take a beat before casting their votes for the leadership structure. "Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank discussion about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here," Banks said in a statement. TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING But Republican leadership had already planned for a meeting heading into the elections, and part of Thune’s popularity among Republicans is his willingness to take feedback from lawmakers rather than "rule with an iron fist," a GOP aide told Fox News Digital. Whether trying to slow down leadership elections turns into a shake-up in the Senate GOP’s power structure remains in the air, even with conservative voices outside the Senate calling for Thune to step aside. So far, Thune is expected to run unopposed for another term and still remains popular among the conference. Possible challengers, like Scott, have already said they wouldn’t mount a bid against him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice," Scott said on Fox News’ "Saturday in America." When pressed if he would support Thune, however, Scott said, "We’ll see what happens." "We’ll see who else is going to run," he said. "I don’t know if somebody else is going to run."

articles.title: Alaska Senate fight heats up as Sullivan moves to block Peltola lawsuit over rejected absentee ballot records
articles.summary: Dan Sullivan's campaign accuses Mary Peltola of trying to "rig the system" by suing Alaska's Division of Elections amid a razor-thin Senate race.
articles.body: Sen. Dan Sullivan's re-election campaign filed a motion to intervene in a lawsuit from Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign on Monday, arguing the lawsuit was seeking to force Alaska elections officials to ignore state law. Sullivan and Peltola remain locked in a razor-thin race for U.S. Senate after last week's election. Peltola's campaign filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections on Friday seeking access to records for absentee ballots that were preliminarily rejected in the midterm election. The Division responded to the lawsuit by stating that individual voters have yet to be notified that their ballots were rejected, and it would be improper to grant Peltola's campaign access to that data before voters themselves. DUNLEAVY CALLS ALASKA VOTING SYSTEM ‘VERY CONFUSING’ AS RAZOR-THIN SENATE RACE FROZEN IN TIME Sullivan's campaign argued on Monday that the lawsuit is an attempt to "rig the system" in Peltola's favor. "It should surprise no one that the same D.C. lawyers who spent more than a year conspiring with Mary Peltola’s campaign to deceive Alaskan voters are now asking a court to let her campaign ignore Alaska law and change the rules while votes are still being counted," said Nate Adams, campaign spokesman. "Peltola’s lawsuit is only further evidence that she is not confident she can win on the merits alone, which is why her campaign is once again attempting to rig the system in her favor." ALASKA VOTERS APPEAR POISED TO PRESERVE RANKED-CHOICE VOTING AMID 'DECOY DAN' SENATE DRAMA "Our campaign is following Alaska precedent to make sure every legally cast ballot is counted, and we remain confident that when every one of those ballots is counted, Senator Sullivan will win," Adams continued. As of Monday, Peltola leads Sullivan by just over 600 votes, with over 25% of votes remaining to be counted. PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING' Sullivan and the GOP have condemned Democrats for a "Decoy Dan" scheme that saw an independent, Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot in an alleged plot to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent. Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the other Sullivan tried to get on the general election ballot as Daniel S. Sullivan, using the middle initial of the incumbent instead of his own. SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’ "That kind of opened our eyes and we began an investigation back there, the Division of Elections did, to determine if this was a legitimate candidacy, and the Division of Elections at that time found that was not and did not put him on the ballot," Dunleavy said. "Then there was a court case and the Supreme Court in the end ruled against the Division of Elections in Alaska, and they must go on the ballot." articles.title: Mississippi Senate latest: Scott Colom's lead over Cindy Hyde-Smith tops 2,500 votes as key deadlines loom
articles.summary: Ballots are still being counted, but Colom's lead has grown by more than 2,500 votes since Election Day.
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom's lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the uncalled Mississippi Senate race had grown to 2,574 votes on Monday, according to the Associated Press , ahead of key deadlines this week to finalize the results.

Outstanding ballots are due by Tuesday, Nov. 10. County clerks have until Nov. 13 to certify the election. And Colom's lead has widened almost every day since Election Day, when it stood at just 65 votes.

Even though 97% of the vote is in, the AP has yet to call the race because the gap between Colom and Hyde-Smith remains narrow — just 0.28% of all ballots cast.

Colom has continually expressed confidence that his campaign will prevail, flooding the airwaves and attending at least eight events over the last few days. "It's very clear the direction of this," he told reporters on Friday . "[Cindy Hyde-Smith] needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn't have one."

In contrast, Hyde-Smith "has not been seen publicly since she left her election night watch party just outside of Jackson," according to CNN .

Along with Alaska — which also remains too close to call — the outcome in Mississippi will determine whether Democrats can expand their new Senate majority beyond its current size (54 seats) by flipping even more red states than they already have .

But Alaska was supposed to be a toss-up . Mississippi — one of the reddest states in the country — wasn't really on the national radar. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a "likely Republican" hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it .

Yet, here we are, with Colom edging Hyde-Smith as lawyers, operatives and legal observers descend on Mississippi to watch officials count every last ballot. How did the Mississippi Senate race get so close — and what happens next?

Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus.

In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases.

In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination.

"I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times .

But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ."

In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper."

Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy.

Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since.

There were signs before Election Day that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%.

Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn.

Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from."

In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 14 million views on Colom's X account .

When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own).

In the end, it wasn't enough to give Hyde-Smith a decisive victory on Election Day. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom went to his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

"I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for."

According to preliminary New York Times estimates , Colom performed 19 points better among white Mississippi voters than Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. He won new voters — that is, those who didn't vote in 2024 — by 25 points.

The contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith hasn't been called yet because officials are still tallying two remaining batches of ballots.

The first batch contains mail-in absentee ballots, which must be postmarked by Election Day and arrive by Tuesday, Nov. 10. The other batch contains affidavit ballots, which were generally cast by people who did not present an acceptable photo ID at the polls or who had been marked as inactive on voter rolls. Voters also have until 5 p.m. local time on Tuesday, Nov. 10, to validate their affidavit ballots with an acceptable ID.

County clerks in Mississippi then have until Friday, Nov. 13, to certify the election.

The Colom campaign has said that roughly 15,000 affidavit ballots were cast this year. Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said late last week that there were as many as 20,000 outstanding ballots of all kinds — including more than 3,000 mail-in ballots — and that about half them had been processed by midday Friday .

Colom's team believes his lead will expand once all the outstanding ballots are counted. (It has already grown by more than 2,500 votes since Election Day.) Ahead of Mississippi's March primaries, incorrect Experian information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters — and inactivations have more than doubled in some jurisdictions since then. Discrepancies caused confusion and long lines at polling places on Tuesday, forcing affected voters to cast affidavit ballots.

"We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat," Colom wrote on X on Wednesday morning . He added on Thursday that "my campaign, alongside the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] and Elias Law Group, Lisa Ross, and our great team of local attorneys, are leading the effort to ensure every eligible voter is heard."

Hyde-Smith also expressed confidence on Election Night. "We still don't have all the votes in, so we're not calling all of it tonight, but we're in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator," she told supporters at the time.

On Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party chairman Mike Hurst said he was "enthusiastic about these outstanding ballots because a number of these, a significant number of these, we believe, are in and remain in Republican-leaning districts, precincts and counties throughout the state."

Mississippi is the only state in the country without a recount law. But if the margin is still razor-close next week, Colom or Hyde-Smith could challenge certain ballots in court. That would likely happen after certification on Nov. 13.

Lawyers for Hyde-Smith and her campaign have formally written to Mississippi state officials to demand "the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots," according to the New York Times — a signal that they may pursue litigation if those ballots put Colom over the top.

Hurst added on Thursday that lawyers aligned with Hyde-Smith "will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal, if there is evidence that the law has been violated."

articles.title: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie unveils impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. war with Iran and other military actions ordered by President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. war with Iran and other military actions ordered by President Donald Trump. House GOP leaders will be forced to bring the impeachment articles up for a floor vote within two legislative days because Massie filed the measure as privileged under House rules. Republicans could also make a motion to kill the resolution, which would require a majority vote. A simple majority vote is required in the House for the articles to be approved. If the effort is successful, the resolution is then sent to the Senate to decide whether to convict and remove Hegseth from office. Massie, a longtime Trump critic who’s retiring from Congress at the end of the year, brought eight charges against Hegseth, accusing him of “waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat.” Hegseth “has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as secretary of defense,” Massie said as he read the articles on the House floor, adding that Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law.” The first article “charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat,” according to Massie’s announcement. “It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception.” Congress has the power to declare war under Article 1 of the Constitution, though the last time it formally declared war was World War II. The 1973 War Powers Resolution requires that the president formally notify the House speaker and Senate president pro tempore within two days any time the military is used and war hasn’t been declared. The law also requires the president to end the use of armed forces within 60 days if he uses the military without prior notification to Congress. Massie, who originally introduced the articles in September, said that Hegseth “abused the powers of his high office” by “directing, authorizing, and sustaining hostile United States military actions in Iran after the expiration of the 60-day period.” Since the early 2000s, presidents from both parties, including Trump, have relied on authorizations for the use of military force approved by Congress to order military action without the green light from lawmakers. Massie’s articles of impeachment also include charges related to alleged “extrajudicial killings,” referring to the strikes on alleged drug boats; “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader,” referring to the U.S. capturing then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro; and “unlawful war in Yemen.” Hegseth said Monday that he will hold a press conference Tuesday morning to address efforts to impeach him. When asked by reporters whether he has enough Republican support to defeat an impeachment, Hegseth said, “We’re not worried about that.” “We’re going to do a press conference tomorrow at the Pentagon on that very topic,” he continued. “So I’ll save my remarks there. I hope you’ll all come loaded for bear with your questions.” On Sunday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he was a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Hegseth. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries said. The House last impeached a federal officer in 2024 when it approved articles against then-Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas under President Joe Biden on charges related to his handling of the border. But the Democratic-led Senate voted to dismiss the charges. Voter backlash to the Iran war and the resulting rise in oil prices appeared to play a major role in Democrats’ successful midterm election last week. Trump and Vice President JD Vance both blamed GOP losses on the conflict, which began in late February with joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Trump questions midterm election results after previously accepting outcome
articles.summary: President Trump made new allegations about Democrats' historic midterm rout without evidence, again making unsubstantiated voter fraud accusations.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON − President Donald Trump cast doubt on the results of the midterm election, pushing unsubstantiated accusations of rigged election machines in a social media post after previously accepting the blowout defeat for Republicans .

Like he has in previous elections, Trump on Nov. 9 reverted to making baseless assertions of voter fraud to explain last week's midterm triumph for Democrats.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump said in a post on Truth Social . "How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting 'dumps' were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!"

Despite Trump suggesting midterm polls were "wrong," the vast majority of public surveys forecast a midterm blue tsunami that resulted in Democrats taking control of the House and Senate, flipping double-digit Republican House districts, and winning Senate races in historically Republican states such as Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Election officials across the country have also not raised major concerns about early-voting discrepancies or voting machines in the 2026 races. Trump's accusations come as Republican officials oversee elections in many of the reliably red states where Democrats found success for the first time in decades.

Trump has a long history of denying election results when he or other Republicans lose and alleging voter fraud without evidence. Most notably, he worked to overturn his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden after making groundless voter-fraud claims, which came before the Jan. 6, 2021 storming of the U.S. Capitol by Trump supporters. He refuses to accept the 2020 defeat to this date.

In other interviews since last week's midterm election, Trump has acknowledged the sweeping defeat for his party, which has been widely interpreted by political observers as a forceful repudiation of Trump's second term, particularly over his handling of the economy and the war in Iran.

Candidates make history in race, gender and faith in 2026

On the night of the Nov. 3 midterm election, Trump told The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the result of the midterm elections and said he looked forward to "working with" Democrats in Congress.

In an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" that aired on Nov. 8, Trump also acknowledged the election defeats of Republicans, arguing they struggled because he wasn't on the ballot and because of the Iran war.

"I think if I was on the ballot it would have been a much different situation," Trump said. "But there's something beyond that. They didn't like the war. They didn't like the fact that gasoline went up."

images.caption: President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One en route to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, at President Donald J. Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, US, November 8, 2026.

The Midterms marked historic firsts across race, gender, religion and sexual orientation. Scroll to see who made history this election. The Peach State's gubernatorial contest also went the Democrats way, electing former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Bottoms as the nation's first Black woman governor by about 9 percentage points. She will be first Democrat elected to lead Georgia since 1998. Democrats flipped at least seven seats in the Senate to gain a 54-seat majority in traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. (Carlos Barria, REUTERS)
Democrat Annie Andrews became the first woman Senator elected in South Carolina. (Win McNamee, Getty Images)
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed beat his GOP opponent , becoming the nation's first Muslim U.S. senator. (Ryan Garza, USA TODAY Network)
Democrat David Crowley won Wisconsin’s governor race, becoming the first Black person to hold the office. (Jovanny Hernandez / Milwaukee Journal Sentinel)
Florida Democrat Pia Dandiya notched a historic first after becoming the first Indian American to be elected to Congress in the Sunshine state. (CRYSTAL VANDER WEIT/TCPALM)

Democrat Deb Haaland of New Mexico made history after being elected the first Native American woman to serve as a governor of any state. She previously made history as the first Native American woman in Congress and the first Native American woman in the Biden administration cabinet. (Jasper Colt, USA TODAY)
In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, won the race to become the first Native American woman in the Senate. (TIM EVANS, AFP via Getty Images)

articles.title: Arizona Republican holds House seat, surviving re-election scare
articles.summary: Republican Rep. Eli Crane thanked rural Arizonans and vowed to fight the status quo in Congress after defeating Jonathan Nez in their Arizona rematch.
articles.body: Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz., narrowly won re-election to a second term, defeating Democratic challenger Jonathan Nez in a tight rematch, The Associated Press projected Monday. Crane, a former Navy SEAL combat veteran, previously defeated Nez, a former president of the Navajo Nation, in the 2024 general election. Crane and Nez were separated by 3,834 votes at the time of the AP race call. The Fox News Power Rankings had rated the seat Likely R in the lead-up to Election Day. Nez has not yet conceded the race. His most recent social media post, from Nov. 5, said that counting every ballot "takes time" in the large district. BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS In a post on X, Crane thanked rural Arizonans and his staff while praising Nez for stepping into the arena again. "I'm going to keep fighting against the status quo in Congress," Crane wrote. "Both parties have been driving this country into the ground for decades, and the American people are sick of it." TRUMP TORCHES DEMOCRATS AT ARIZONA RALLY, WARNS THEY WILL ‘DESTROY OUR COUNTRY’ AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Crane was backed by President Donald Trump, who endorsed the GOP lawmaker as an "America First Patriot." At the same time, Trump targeted Nez, labeling him a "Radical Left Democrat" who opposes eliminating taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING "He wants massive Tax Increases, Open Borders, Men playing in Women’s Sports, and Transgender Mutilation of your Children. Jonathan Nez is Reckless, Radical, and Dangerous!" Trump wrote. articles.title: Supreme Court paves way for Trump to build a section of his border wall in the Big Bend area of Texas
articles.summary: The Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to move forward with construction of his border wall in the remote Big Bend region of southwest Texas.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday allowed President Donald Trump to move forward with construction of his border wall in the remote Big Bend region of southwest Texas. Construction there had been challenged by an environmental group and locals who say it would damage the environment and historic sites. The justices blocked an injunction imposed by a federal judge in Texas that had blocked construction while litigation continues. In a five-page unsigned decision, the court said that the federal judge who ruled on the issue had no authority to do so, adding that the Trump administration was “extremely likely to prevail” on that point. The government, the court added, has “compelling interests” when a challenged policy involves border security. Of the nine justices, only liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. The segment of the border adjacent to the Rio Grande is sparsely populated, with the Trump administration saying that 89,000 people have been detained trying to enter the United States there in recent years. The section in question, which the government says would involve 341 miles of construction, includes Big Bend National Park. The legal dispute focuses on three waivers issued by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in February and her successor Markwayne Mullin in May and July that allowed the government to evade environmental and conservation laws. In a court filing, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said Congress in 1996 gave the government “broad authority” to build border infrastructure without getting tied up in red tape. The move was challenged by the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group; Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit group dedicated to restoring a historic church in the area; and Danny Miller, a river guide who owns property in the area. Lawyers for the challengers said that if construction goes ahead, it would “result in the permanent alteration of an irreplaceable landscape” and “threaten unique historic and cultural resources.” Contrary to the government’s assertions, the Big Bend area has “the lowest apprehension rates” for migrants anywhere along the border, they added. Government data shows that Big Bend has the section of the southern border with the lowest number of encounters between federal agents and migrants. The plaintiffs say that the 1996 law only allows for limited waivers for border construction projects in areas where illegal crossings are pervasive. U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 invalidated Noem’s waivers, saying the secretary lacked such sweeping powers. Cardone declined to put her ruling on hold, prompting the administration to turn to the Supreme Court. Trump’s pledge to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has been one of his signature policies ever since his first presidential campaign in 2016. It is part of his hard-line immigration policy that focuses on border security and mass deportations. Officials have warned that if other parts of the wall are built but the Big Bend area remains open, it would be exploited by those seeking to enter the country illegally. Boosted by construction funding from the Republican-controlled Congress, the administration seeks to fulfill Trump’s plan by completing a 2,000-mile installation including steel panels, vehicle barriers and new surveillance technology.

articles.title: Rubio's defense of Trump's Iran war draws sharp contrast with Vance's midterm blame
articles.summary: JD Vance blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm losses, raising questions about his 2028 ambitions and his shift from Trump on the conflict.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration's war against Iran on Sunday, days after Vice President JD Vance blamed the conflict for Republicans' devastating midterm losses, as the White House confronts an unresolved standoff with Tehran. "I think the president took on something that other presidents have failed to do. Sometimes, when you do the right thing, you don't know whether it's popular or not, but it's still the right thing to do. Presidents are elected to take on the hard things, sometimes difficult things, but necessary things," Rubio said Sunday. Vance made his argument in a post on X last week. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote last week. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," he added. VANCE REFUSES TO PUT A CLOCK ON IRAN CONFLICT AS KEY QUESTION KEEPS US FORCES ENGAGED Vance cited an unnamed pollster in the X post who said voters who had abandoned the GOP wanted the administration to end the conflict, address inflation and the cost of living, put America first and change its relationship with Israel. The vice president's argument that the war was the primary driver of Republicans' losses, however, is complicated by polling. The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who said the same about the war in Iran. The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two issues may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections. Fox News Digital contacted Vance's office five times seeking clarification on whether ending the conflict would mean lifting the blockade, withdrawing American forces or securing new concessions from Tehran, but received no response. The contrasting assessments come as Republicans begin looking ahead to 2028, with Trump naming Rubio as a possible presidential contender during an interview with CBS. Some longtime Trump donors are reportedly expressing doubts about backing Vance in 2028, fearing his ties to the Trump administration and the GOP’s devastating midterm losses could hurt his presidential prospects, with some floating Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and other Republicans as alternatives, according to The Wall Street Journal. Meanwhile, Trump and Vance are pursuing another diplomatic opening with Iran, with Qatar mediating talks over a possible agreement that could ease the U.S. blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump met with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani Monday to discuss mediation efforts and potential terms for ending the conflict with Iran. Rubio expressed skepticism Sunday that negotiations were nearing a breakthrough, arguing that Iran's demands remained unrealistic. Vance has been personally involved in indirect talks with Iranian representatives through regional mediators in recent weeks, according to Axios. "I’m not in a political office," Rubio told reporters Sunday when asked about the midterm results. "As you know, I just don’t comment on domestic politics." TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES Trump initially projected that Operation Epic Fury, launched against Iran in February, would involve four to five weeks of combat operations. More than eight months later, the broader confrontation continues despite the end of major U.S. combat operations in April. After a June Memorandum of Understanding with Iran failed to produce a lasting resolution, the Trump administration returned to economic and military pressure, with renewed limited strikes, continued maritime tensions and an unresolved standoff over Iranian missile capabilities and the flow of oil and natural gas through the Strait of Hormuz. Vance played a role in the administration's negotiations with Iran, helping lead diplomatic efforts that produced the June agreement before it unraveled. Trump even joked in June that Vance would take the blame if the Iran deal failed. "If it works out, I'm going to take the credit. If it doesn't work out, I'm blaming JD," Trump said at the time. The vice president has previously defended the administration's military campaign, crediting U.S. forces with significantly weakening Iran's conventional military and its ability to threaten commercial shipping. "The VP has let it be known for a few months now that he is not in full agreement with the President on Iran. But [the] social media post is striking, if not shocking," Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute's Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East, told Fox News Digital. Hood also questioned Vance's emphasis on the war as the primary cause of Republicans' losses, arguing that broader economic concerns played a significant role in voters' frustration. AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? Trump dismissed suggestions that Vance's comments about Iran had strained their relationship on Sunday, defending Vance's remarks while suggesting he should have gone a step further in expressing support for the administration's actions. "No, not at all," Trump said when asked whether Vance's comments had affected their relationship. "But a lot of people didn't like his comments, but not me. He was right." Trump added that Vance "should have made one other statement," arguing that the administration's actions against Iran were worth repeating. TRUMP'S IRAN GAMBLE DIVIDES GOP HAWKS AND 'AMERICA FIRST' CONSERVATIVES OVER WHAT VICTORY LOOKS LIKE Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also publicly defended the Iran campaign, calling it a "courageous and historic" effort even as Vance questions its political costs. Hegseth also faces questions about his future in the administration, although the president publicly insisted he intends to keep his Pentagon chief. Beyond the political fallout, assessments differ over whether the administration has achieved its military objectives and what risks remain for the United States. GOP CRACKS WIDEN OVER IRAN WAR AS VULNERABLE CANDIDATES BREAK WITH TRUMP, DEMAND ITS END Retired Army Lt. Col. Daniel L. Davis, a veteran of four combat deployments and host of the "Daniel Davis Deep Dive" show on YouTube, offered a sharply critical assessment of the campaign's results, arguing that the administration has failed to accomplish the objectives Trump outlined when the operation began. On Feb. 28, Trump pledged to destroy Iran's missile capabilities and production facilities, eliminate its navy and prevent Tehran's regional proxies from destabilizing the Middle East. "Eight months and 9 days later, none of those objectives have been met," Davis told Fox News Digital. The White House has offered a starkly different assessment. In April, the administration declared that U.S. forces had achieved the military objectives of Operation Epic Fury, pointing to the destruction of Iranian military infrastructure and significant degradation of Tehran's missile and naval capabilities. Davis said that although American strikes inflicted significant damage on Iran's conventional military, Tehran retains the ability to threaten U.S. forces and regional allies through missiles, drones and naval assets protected in underground facilities. He warned that renewed major combat operations could expose American forces and Gulf allies to further retaliation without eliminating those capabilities. VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' "First, it should be clear: shooting the same targets, with the same missiles, is not going to produce a different outcome," Davis said. "Can't put lipstick on this pig: it would be ugly and seen as an admission of defeat," Davis said. "But that is still profoundly better for our interests than going back to combat ops that will only deepen, significantly, the cost of our failure." Hood, however, rejected the suggestion that the United States should abandon pressure on Tehran, arguing that Iran continues to pose a serious threat to regional stability and American interests. "Trump seems to get that Iran, as currently governed, is a singularly dangerous threat to the region's stability and ability to prosper; is, has long been, a source of international terrorism; and would be even more dangerous with nuclear weapons," Hood said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hood said the administration needs to more clearly explain its strategic objectives, including whether Washington is seeking significant concessions on Iran's nuclear program or a political shift in Tehran. "The administration's messaging to the America people and to international partners needs improvement. What are our strategic objectives?" Hood said. Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment.
